items.title: Interoperable Provenance Contribution (IPC): A Candidate PROV-Aligned Application Profile for Contribution Traceability
items.abstract: This exploratory research paper proposes Interoperable Provenance Contribution (IPC), a candidate application profile grounded in W3C PROV for tracing human, AI, software and data contributions across systems. It presents six candidate evidentiary requirements, a preliminary event model, a comparison with existing technical standards and three synthetic research cases. Version 2.3, 31 October 2026. Not peer reviewed. Production interoperability and independent conformance have not yet been validated. Companion Research Materials Interactive demonstration: https://huggingface.co/spaces/GBSNResearch/ipc-provenance-explorer GitHub repository (source code and synthetic datasets): https://github.com/gbsn-research/IPC-Interoperable-Contribution-Provenance Zenodo research archive: https://zenodo.org/records/24281403 These materials illustrate the proposed IPC event representation and contribution-traceability model using synthetic examples. They do not establish production-grade provenance capture or independently validated cross-platform interoperability.

items.title: Is This Code Mine? Student Ownership When AI Agents Write the Spec and the Code
items.abstract: Software engineering courses are starting to ask students to build entire systems with AI coding agents, but little is known about what students actually do with them and whether they still own what they deliver. If the agent writes both the code and the decisions behind it, the artifacts we grade no longer show what students learned. We studied an assignment in which 18 pairs of students built applications with agents under Spec-Driven Development, combining the mined history of their repositories, the prompts they recorded, and a survey of 33 students. The agents wrote 69\% of the specifications meant to keep students in control, sometimes from a prompt of a few words. Students locate their ownership in the ideas, crediting themselves with half of them but a fifth of the code, yet most could not explain that code to a colleague or modify it without the agent, and what they report having written is unrelated to what their own commits declare. The three teams that met the 100,000-line target did so with generated code the application never uses, in one case proposed by the agent itself, and one team rewrote its history to backdate its specifications. Teaching with agents should therefore assess what students specify, review, and can explain, rather than what they ship, and enforce the engineering process with tools rather than trusting it to students or agents.

items.title: Jetriever: Shifting Agent Memory Retrieval from Similarity to Utility
items.abstract: Whether a stored memory helps answer a user's question often depends on world knowledge rather than surface similarity. Jetriever replaces similarity search with full-pool utility scoring: given a query, it uses Jev, an LLM-derived System One decision model, to score every stored memory for the probability that it is useful to the answer, ranking the memory pool directly by those probabilities. On InMind's 125 indirect-query tasks, Jetriever places the gold exchange first in 84.8% of cases (versus 1.6% for BM25 and 0.0% for MiniLM with user-turn indexing) and reaches 76.0% end-to-end Application, compared with at most 16.0% across published retrieval and memory systems. A controlled 20-question comparison disentangles recognizing implicit evidence from ranking it properly: Jev and Qwen3.5-9B both recover 90% of gold exchanges within the top 50 (versus 30% for the BERT-based decision model Laya), yet at rank 1 Jev reaches 85% while Qwen3.5-9B drops to 40%. On a dimension-proportional random sample of 60 MemoryAgentBench questions, Jetriever raises the four-dimension average from 44.3% (ReFind) to 55.4%, at a mean retrieval cost of USD 0.00834 per InMind query and USD 0.03103 per MAB query. Together, these results show that effective utility retrieval hinges on combining broad world knowledge, calibrated ranking probabilities, and affordable full-pool evaluation.

items.title: Jev-as-a-Reward: Validating Probabilistic Safety Judges for Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Probabilistic safety judges return the probability of a safety label and cheaply score reinforcement learning rollouts. A confidence gate sends only uncertain verdicts to a stronger LLM judge, which leaves confidently passed harm in a blind spot. Policies can exploit this blind spot, and commercial judges release new versions. We propose a protocol that validates such a judge before and during training, separates the share of confidently passed harm from its amount, and re-validates it after each judge change. We apply it to two versions of Jev, a commercial decision-only judge, and to an open guard classifier. Under the probability reward of Jev, passed harm shrinks in all 11 runs under the primary reference, mostly more slowly than caught harm, and concentrates in the blind spot. Binarizing this judge meets the escape criterion on Llama, and the open guard classifier shows an escape signal in one seed under a second reference. Guard classifiers share this blind spot, and even frontier LLM judges catch at most one of 10 human-labeled confident misses. Without a trained reward model, the probability reward with a helpfulness term lowers HarmBench attack success on Llama-3.1-8B from 0.287 to at most 0.033 at the final checkpoint.

items.title: k-Nearest Neighbours: Homophily and the Making of Difference
items.abstract: This chapter presents a sociotechnical analysis of k-nearest neighbours (kNN) algorithm, following the same diagrammatic method. First, the description of statistical formulation and operational logic of kNN is introduced. Then, historical genealogy is presented, tracing the lineage of kNN back to nearest neighbour rule in optics and heuristics (Occam’s Razor), as well as connecting this lineage to sociological research on homophily and the spatial logic of difference. The chapter argues that as an operational diagram kNN modulates differences through organizing them into partitions based on relations of similarity and dis/connection, while materializing homophilic principles of sociality and segregation that permeate network science.

items.title: Knowledge Transfer and Talent Development in Traditional Craftsmanship: An HRM Perspective from Atlas Silk
items.abstract: Based on 30 named individual cases documented in public media reports, this paper analyzes the knowledge structure, transmission pathways and talent development challenges associated with Atlas Silk craftsmanship from a human resource management perspective. The B1-B11 framework is used to summarize knowledge content and training arrangements, and the C1-C10 framework is used to identify training, retention and job support issues. The results show that the process and material knowledge can be incorporated into structured training, and the embodied experience of warping, dyeing and weaving still depends on long-term field practice. Families, workshops, cooperatives, colleges and digital communication have complementary functions. To support talent succession, we should combine the phased ability development, compensation guarantee, whole process rotation, dual-mentor training and work design that takes into account the family situation. This paper is a purposively selected literature-based case study, which is not statistically representative.

items.title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
items.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.

items.title: LEAF-OPD: Learning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation
items.abstract: LLM unlearning aims to erase targeted knowledge from large language models while preserving their utility. However, many existing methods suppress target knowledge without explicitly teaching the model how to respond to queries about it. We propose LEAF-OPD (LEArning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation), in which a frozen teacher provides token-level supervision on student-generated responses. On forget data, the teacher uses privileged contexts (instructions not to reveal knowledge about forget targets) to guide forgetting. On retain data, the teacher provides supervision without privileged context to preserve model utility. The student operates without privileged context in both cases, learning how to respond when encountering knowledge that should be forgotten. A key challenge is that the teacher often provides effective supervision only at the first few tokens of student trajectories. We introduce Supervision Signal (SS) to measure corrective supervision over a specified token interval, evaluating the entire trajectory (SS1) and its second half (SS0.5) to assess overall strength and late-stage persistence. When supervision is weak, lightweight SFT strengthens the teacher's context-conditioned refusal behavior, substantially increasing both scores. We evaluate LEAF-OPD on three widely used benchmarks: TOFU, RWKU, and MUSE-News. On TOFU, LEAF-OPD achieves the best Forget Quality, Model Utility, and Forget ROUGE-L while maintaining competitive retain performance. On RWKU, it outperforms the second-best method by 34% in Forget Quality while maintaining competitive Retain Quality. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of privileged-context supervision with on-policy token-level distillation for LLM unlearning.

items.title: Learning from Distribution: Rethinking One-Hot Supervision for ASR and QA in Speech Language Models
items.abstract: Speech language models (SLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in automatic speech recognition (ASR) and general-purpose speech understanding, yet ASR-specific training often degrades spoken question answering (QA) performance. We revisit this conflict from the perspective of task-specific input--output mappings and one-hot supervision. Our findings reveal pronounced task-asymmetric effects: ASR-only training severely limits QA capability, whereas QA-only training retains reasonable ASR performance. We hypothesize that the relatively deterministic mapping of ASR, combined with single-reference supervision, biases models toward transcription-specific behavior. Motivated by this perspective, we advocate broadening ASR learning objectives while preserving recognition accuracy. We propose Learning from Distribution (LFD), which aligns speech-conditioned predictions with the conditional output distributions of a pretrained text LLM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LFD improves both ASR and QA performance, exhibits superior data efficiency, and remains effective under full-parameter fine-tuning. CoT-ASR further supports the broader applicability of our proposed supervision principle.

items.title: Learning In-Context Adaptivity for LLMs through Continual Gameplay
items.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon tasks where they must explore, gather experience, and adapt their decisions accordingly. We name this capability in-context adaptivity: improving decisions across episodes from experience accumulated in context. We propose to evaluate it in repeated imperfect-information games against unknown opponents. In these games, fixed game-theoretically optimal policies cannot achieve maximum reward, whereas adapting to the opponent increases returns across games. We design a paired protocol that evaluates each agent with and without memory under identical conditions to isolate experience gain from single-game skill. Evaluation shows that memory brings little performance gain for open-weight models and inconsistent gains for frontier models. Our analysis of the agents' summaries and actions identifies a memory-doing gap in which models accurately record opponent tendencies yet rarely depart from default play. To close this gap, we construct a pool of exploitable opponents and post-train Qwen3.5-9B with supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning. We optimize full-match return across context segments so summary generation and action selection are trained together. On unseen opponents, our 9B RL policy doubles experience gain over supervised fine-tuning in Leduc Hold'em and increases it fivefold in No-Limit Hold'em. Across 35 opponents, our policy matches or surpasses frontier models, generalizes beyond its training horizon, and retains most of its gain on summaries from frontier models.

items.title: Learning to Reason with Predictive Gains for Generative Recommendation
items.abstract: Reasoning-enhanced generative recommendation (GR) has attracted increasing attention for leveraging the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to improve next-item prediction. However, existing methods primarily optimize reasoning through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards determined by final recommendation performance, which faces two key limitations: (i) unmeasured predictive contributions within reasoning, where the predictive contributions of individual reasoning steps are not directly reflected in optimization signals, and (ii) weakly discriminative learning signals within groups, where different reasoning trajectories within the group often receive indistinguishable rewards, limiting effective policy optimization. In this paper, we propose GainReason, a simple yet effective training framework that optimizes reasoning through Predictive Gain (PG). Specifically, PG measures changes in target Semantic ID (SID) log-likelihood induced by individual reasoning sentences, providing contribution-aware and discriminative rewards. We further theoretically establish the alignment between expected PG and the recommendation ranking objective. Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.

items.title: Leverage-Enhanced Sampling Owen Method for Explainable Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Recently, the Shapley value has been widely applied in machine learning for feature importance analysis and model explainability. The multilinear extension of games proposed by Owen (1972) expresses the Shapley value as the integral of partial derivatives along the main diagonal of the cube. Direct evaluation of this integral requires exponential-time computation of the partial derivatives. To improve computational efficiency, we propose a sampling-based estimation strategy within Owen's multilinear extension framework, combining stratified sampling with coalition leverage scores. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining explanation accuracy.

items.title: Lift, See, Act: Hierarchical Robot Policy Pretraining with 3D Foundation Models
items.abstract: Robot policy pretraining based on human videos is crucial for improving the policy's generalization ability. One main challenge for this task is the lack of explicit action-relevant representations in such unlabeled data. Recent works tend to estimate 3D hand motion trajectories from videos using 3D foundation models (3D FMs). However, they keep solely the sparse trajectories as supervision, ignoring the rich, fine-grained information produced during the trajectory extraction process. To address this issue, we propose LSA, a hierarchical robot policy pretraining framework that includes three phases: Lift, See, and Act. Specifically, the Lift phase elevates 2D video observations into dense 3D representations by adaptively aligning features in the policy's shallow layers with the intermediate representations extracted from multiple 3D FMs. Building upon these lifted representations, the See phase equips the policy with explicit geometric and interactive awareness through dual guidance. It introduces depth-map reconstruction to help the model comprehend 3D spatial layouts and utilizes hand region cues to explicitly supervise the encoder's attention toward task-relevant interaction hotspots. Empowered by the dense 3D representation learning and precise spatial guidance, our policy achieves robust and accurate robotic manipulation in the Act phase. Extensive experiments on diverse simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that LSA significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. The project page is available at: https://yiyuan00.github.io/Lift-See-Act.

items.title: Linear Regression: From Regression to the Mean to Relation Machines
items.abstract: Chapter 3 presents a sociotechnical analysis of linear regression as an operational diagram. It introduces the logical and statistical formulation of linear regression and delves into the history of this method, particularly its conceptualization by Francis Galton, connecting this history to the notions of normality and averages in statistics. The entanglements of the conception of normality and Galton’s work with eugenics are explored. The chapter connects this historical context and the workings of linear regression as an operational diagram by presenting an argument that linear regression in its operations and through its historical, primarily eugenics-oriented contexts actualizes the norming linear thinking by constructing the line of best fit, defining difference in relation to the norm.

items.title: Listening and Mirroring: The Effects of Verbal Attunement and Behavioral Mimicry on Social and Empathic Perceptions of Embodied AI Agents in VR
items.abstract: As embodied agents take on increasingly social and relational roles in VR, visual realism and embodiment alone may be insufficient; users must also perceive these agents as emotionally attuned, supportive, and humanlike. Prior work suggests that verbal attunement and nonverbal mimicry can each improve users’ social evaluations of embodied agents. However, behavioral mimicry has largely been studied outside of real-time, conversational AI interactions, leaving limited understanding of how users respond when an agent simultaneously generates contextually responsive dialogue and adapts its nonverbal behavior during an immersive conversation. To address this gap, we developed an embodied AI counselor that combines conversational AI with real-time facial-expression and posture mimicry, while producing either verbally attuned or neutral responses. We evaluated the system in a 2 × 2 within-subjects study with 20 participants, manipulating verbal attunement and behavioral mimicry. Results showed that verbal attunement was the most reliable driver of perceived empathy. Behavioral mimicry showed a marginal relationship with perceived humanness, while greater mimicry exposure showed preliminary, exploratory positive associations with empathy, positivity, and humanness, particularly among female participants. Together, these findings show that multimodal synchrony is not a simple additive strategy for designing empathic conversational agents in VR and underscore the need to consider how verbal and nonverbal behaviors are combined during real-time interaction.

items.title: LLM-Driven Automatic Reward Optimization for Ambient Intelligence Robots with Curriculum Interference Auto-Correction
items.abstract: Service robots in ambient intelligence (AmI) scenarios such as smart factories and home services must rapidly adapt to diverse manipulation tasks, yet traditional reinforcement learning (RL) reward design heavily relies on domain expertise, requiring days to weeks of manual tuning. Existing LLM-assisted reward design methods assume that generated rewards can be directly applied to training environments, overlooking potential incompatibility with built-in training mechanisms such as curriculum learning. To our knowledge, this is the first study to quantify the signal interference phenomenon between LLM-generated rewards and curriculum dynamic weight adjustments---experiments reveal that curriculum modules amplify penalty weights from an initial $-1\times10^{-4}$ to $-0.1$ (a factor of 1000$\times$), overwhelming the positive reward signals---and it proposes an automatic detection and correction mechanism based on feedback ratio anomaly detection. A unified dual-paradigm framework adapting to both ManagerBasedRL and DirectRL paradigms on the IsaacLab platform, along with a humanized interaction paradigm for non-expert users, are also developed. Systematic experiments on five robot tasks of varying difficulty, including ablation studies, 8-sample random search baselines, and multi-seed statistical tests, demonstrate: on Franka Lift the success rate increases from 0\% to 84\%$\pm$2\% and the mean reward from 0.90 to 84.41$\pm$5.50, where simply disabling the curriculum yields a roughly 5$\times$ increase in mean reward (0.90$\rightarrow$4.47)---a necessary prerequisite for LLM reward optimization to take effect---and combining it with the LLM-designed multi-stage reward structure multiplies the improvement by a further 18.9$\times$; under an equal-compute random-search comparison, LLM weight optimization achieves a 47\% improvement over the best random configuration. Mean-reward ratios depend on the reward definition and should be read together with the scale-invariant success rate. items.title: LLM-ES: A Multi-Agent Hybrid Framework Integrating Large Language Models and Expert Systems for Autonomous Cyber Defense
items.abstract: In recent years, Autonomous Cyber Defense (ACD) methods driven by large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising performance in decision interpretability and environmental transferability, yet suffer from low decision efficiency and unstable decision-making. To mitigate these limitations, this work proposes a multi-agent hybrid LLM–expert system framework for ACD. The framework seamlessly integrates the determinism and efficiency of expert systems with the deep reasoning capabilities of LLMs: the expert system makes deterministic decisions based on experiential knowledge, whereas the LLM is responsible for complex decision tasks demanding deep exploration and long-chain reasoning. We further strengthen the LLM via chain-of-thought (CoT) guided prompting, historical memory, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), output alignment and feedback learning. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating the expert system improves both decision efficiency and defense performance. Evaluated on the CybORG CC4 environment, our approach achieves an average reward of − 98 over ten independent rounds, representing an approximate 25.5% improvement over the best-performing reinforcement learning (RL) baseline. Compared with the standalone LLM method, the average reward increases by roughly 96.2%, while the average per-step runtime is reduced by approximately 14.6%. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically integrate LLMs and expert systems for ACD in the CybORG CC4 environment.

items.title: LMM-Incentive: Large Multimodal Model-based Incentive Design for User-Generated Content in Web 3.0
items.abstract: Web 3.0 represents the next generation of the Internet, which is widely recognized as a decentralized ecosystem that focuses on value expression and data ownership. By leveraging blockchain and artificial intelligence technologies, Web 3.0 offers unprecedented opportunities for users to create, own, and monetize their content, thereby enabling User-Generated Content (UGC) to an entirely new level. However, self-interested users may exploit the limitations of content curation mechanisms and generate low-quality content with less effort, obtaining platform rewards under information asymmetry. Such behavior can undermine Web 3.0 performance. To this end, we propose LMM-Incentive , a novel Large Multimodal Model (LMM)-based incentive mechanism for UGC in Web 3.0. Specifically, we propose an LMM-based contract-theoretic model to motivate users to generate high-quality UGC, thereby mitigating the adverse selection problem from information asymmetry. To alleviate potential moral hazards after contract selection, we leverage LMM agents to evaluate UGC quality, which is the primary component of the contract, utilizing prompt engineering techniques to improve the evaluation performance of LMM agents. Recognizing that traditional contract design methods cannot effectively adapt to the dynamic environment of Web 3.0, we develop an improved Mixture of Experts (MoE)-based Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm for optimal contract design. Simulation results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed MoE-based PPO algorithm over representative benchmarks in the context of contract design, where the proposed algorithm achieves a \(5.4\%\) improvement in test rewards over the PPO algorithm. Finally, we deploy the designed contract within an Ethereum smart contract framework, further validating the effectiveness of the proposed scheme.

items.title: LoopROS: A Dual Recursive Self-Improvement Loops of Robotic Operating System Based on Functional Constraints and Trajectory Tuning
items.abstract: Recent advances in foundation models have enabled robotic agents to reason, plan, and adapt their actions through physical interaction. Yet successful execution does not necessarily translate into lasting improvement across tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising paradigm for robotic agents to continuously refine their capabilities through experience, but requires preserving functional knowledge, adapting execution to changing physical conditions, and retaining reusable corrections. We introduce LoopROS, a dual-loop robotic agent framework that couples functionally constrained execution with experience-driven improvement. Within each episode, functional constraint-guided in-context learning identifies essential task relations from demonstrations and context, while visual feedback-guided segmentwise trajectory tuning adapts reference motions through observation-grounded corrections and verification. Across episodes, execution feedback informs revisions to persistent skills, parameters, and executable tools, enabling subsequent executions to reuse corrections under relevant conditions. The LoopROS achieves an 82.0% success rate and a mean score of 88.90, ranking No. 1 in RoboDojo, among the compared methods. We further complete 30 successful trials in three real robot manipulation tasks, elucidating its great potential as a backbone robotic RSI.

items.title: Lost in the Bed: Understanding How Lying Posture and Input Modality Shape Spatial Interaction in Mixed Reality
items.abstract: As mixed reality (MR) systems enter everyday environments, interacting while lying down is an emerging design context. However, existing research has largely focused on supine configurations, overlooking the asymmetric constraints of lateral postures and their interplay with input modality. To address this gap, we conducted a 3 × 2 within-subjects study (N = 36) evaluating pointing performance across three recumbent postures (Supine, Dominant, NonDominant) and two input modalities (Controller and Hand raycasting). Results show that posture effects are strongly moderated by modality: while controller input remained stable, hand input degraded substantially in lateral postures. Furthermore, supported-arm postures increased wrist-rotation demands, whereas unsupported-arm postures led to higher perceived exertion. These findings highlight how posture and modality jointly shape performance and ergonomic burden, informing design considerations for posture-aware recumbent MR interfaces.

items.title: MAGE: Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence for Transferable Multimodal Graph Learning
items.abstract: Multimodal graphs integrate textual and visual attributes with relational structures, providing a rich representation of complex real-world data. To enable the broad applicability and reuse of graph models, it is crucial for models trained on source graphs to generalize to unseen graph domains. However, this is challenging because cross-modal interactions among neighbors and the neighboring information needed for prediction can vary across target nodes and graph domains. This gives rise to two key challenges: adaptive cross-modal neighborhood fusion, which captures and integrates cross-modal interactions among neighbors to accommodate variations across nodes and domains; and target-specific evidence selection, which identifies the neighboring textual and visual information needed for each target node to support LLM-based prediction. In light of these challenges, we propose MAGE (Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence Prompting), a framework for transferable multimodal graph learning. MAGE represents textual and visual node views separately in a heterogeneous graph and introduces two complementary components. Meta-path Adaptive Multimodal Propagation (MAMP) adaptively aggregates neighborhood information along heterogeneous meta-paths and compresses it into graph-aware soft tokens. Evidence-Guided Instruction Tuning (EGIT) selects relevant neighboring evidence for each query and incorporates its graph-aware representations into instructions for a frozen multimodal LLM. Together, these components support transfer from multiple source graphs to unseen target graphs without target-domain parameter updates. Experiments with three source graphs and four unseen target graphs demonstrate strong cross-domain transfer performance on node classification and link prediction, without requiring parameter updates on the target domains.

items.title: Managing safety, functionality, and sustainability of fire-protective clothing: balancing burn prevention, physiological burden, and lifecycle safety
items.abstract: Workers in firefighting, emergency response, aviation, welding, metal processing, and petrochemical operations may be exposed to flame, radiant or convective heat, hot surfaces, molten materials, smoke, and chemical contaminants. Fire-protective clothing is needed when these hazards cannot be fully controlled at source. However, dense multilayer assemblies and chemical treatments can limit heat and moisture loss, increase cardiovascular and metabolic strain, restrict movement, and make cleaning and disposal more difficult. This critical narrative review focuses on structural firefighting and examines research on protective materials, garment engineering, occupational hygiene, ergonomics, thermophysiology, maintenance, and life-cycle management. Studies were selected purposively through a targeted literature update and synthesized across heterogeneous methods and endpoints. Flame resistance at the material level is only one determinant of protection in use. Outcomes also depend on the complete ensemble, wearer, task, environment, and service history. Added insulation can slow external heat transfer while limiting dissipation of metabolic heat; cleaning can remove contaminants but reduce mechanical, barrier, or heat-loss performance; and renewable or recycled content may have limited value if it shortens service life or creates additional chemical and recovery problems. The review proposes a two-stage evaluation approach: first, apply minimum safety requirements that cannot be offset by benefits in other domains; second, compare compliant systems in terms of physiological load, mobility, chemical safety, durability, maintainability, cost, and environmental effects. The synthesis informs condition-based inspection, validated decontamination, representative wear trials, worker input, chemical disclosure, and product-level service records. The framework and proposed service-based sustainability measure require prospective validation; laboratory performance and acute wearer responses do not establish reduced injury or disease incidence.

items.title: MemDoctor: Stage-wise Error Attribution and Repair for MLLM Agent Memory
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now assist users across sessions of images and text, carried by an external memory of what was said and shown. When such an assistant answers wrongly, the failure usually began earlier, in how a record was written, updated or retrieved, and the answer alone does not say where. We formalize multimodal memory as four stages, Write, Update, Retrieve and Answer, and define nine error types across them. A stage-resolved analysis on Mem-Gallery traces most failures to a source stage, and most of those lie before the answer. Injecting known errors against fact-preserving control edits, we then follow each tainted record downstream. Early errors survive to the answer as apparent evidence, and hurt most when no other record holds the fact. A diagnosis that trusts the quoted evidence therefore blames the stage where the error surfaces, not the one where it began. We propose MemDoctor, in which the MLLM that built the memory diagnoses its own failures. It traces each needed fact backward through the four stages, accepts a diagnosis only when the cited evidence is found in memory, and repairs that stage before answering again. On a 4B backbone, MemDoctor improves accuracy on both Mem-Gallery and MemLens, outperforming all evaluated 8B baselines, and the same loop also improves MuRAG and A-Mem.

items.abstract: Sustained cognitive engagement, short and mistimed sleep, chronic stress and reduced recovery co-occur in AI-intensive environments, yet how this profile acts on brain energy metabolism is unknown. We built a neuron–astrocyte genome-scale model of human grey matter from Human-GEM v2.1.1, contextualised each cell with human single-nucleus expression, made transport, sodium-pumping and glutathione-recycling costs explicit, and calibrated one parameter to measured cerebral glucose use. Without further fitting the model reproduced the astrocytic share of oxidative metabolism measured by ¹³C spectroscopy (15.7% vs 14%), both the oxidative and the glycolytic regimes of human brain activation, and an independent reconstruction; deletion of genes causing inherited brain-energy disorders compromised its energetic margin far more often than deletion of other genes (odds ratio 79, p = 6 × 10⁻²⁰). Translating the five stressors into constraints, sleep loss and cognitive load each exhausted the margin within the protocol range, at a 25% loss of mitochondrial capacity and a 39% rise in signalling demand, whereas circadian misalignment, chronic stress and reduced recovery acted on arms with reserve. Combined, the stressors exhausted the margin at 0.72 times the moderate profile; across 400 parameter draws demand was met in 99.2% at low and 28.5% at moderate exposure. Substrate oxidation, not substrate supply, set the margin: restoring sleep or reducing load restored it, whereas ketone bodies, lactate or fibre-derived acetate helped only when glucose delivery itself was limiting. Results held across thresholds, releases, solvers and enzyme-capacity limits, and the thresholds are testable with ³¹P and ¹³C spectroscopy.

items.title: Model Immunization Beyond Condition Numbers: The Importance of Plateau Regions
items.abstract: Harmful fine-tuning can rapidly compromise safety alignment in Large Language Models, underscoring the vulnerability of deployed models to post-release modification. While prior work motivates model immunization by inducing ill-conditioned curvature to slow harmful optimization, this approach is not scalable due to the high computational cost of Hessian estimation. We refine this paradigm by extending the theoretical framework to prioritize plateau regions alongside curvature. We further introduce an immunization algorithm based on efficient Hessian estimation and bounds on the extremal singular values of the Hessian. We demonstrate the proposed immunization framework in three applications: (i) Fine-tuning-as-a-service settings where benign user data may be mixed with poisoned harmful data, (ii) open-weight settings where an adversary can fine-tune on harmful-only data with varied training dynamics, and (iii) robust unlearning, where immunized models better resist relearning attacks after unlearning. Extensive experiments confirm that our approach achieves robust defense against adversarial fine-tuning while largely maintaining general utility and downstream trainability. Our code is available at https://github.com/minhquoc0712/BECON.

items.title: Multi-LLM Agentic AI at the Edge: Joint Agent Scheduling and Resource Allocation
items.abstract: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.

items.title: Multimodal evaluation of cognitive load during prosthetic device use in activities of daily living
items.abstract: The cognitive burden associated with upper-limb prosthesis use remains a barrier to functional adoption, yet existing evaluations often rely on single-modality measures. This study investigates a multimodal framework for assessing cognitive load during activities of daily living. Twelve participants without limb loss performed standardized activities of daily living using their natural hand and a simulated tendon-driven prosthesis in a within-subject design. This controlled baseline was used to evaluate modality-specific responses to prosthesis-mediated task demands across subjective, behavioral, and neurophysiological measures. Cognitive workload was assessed using task performance metrics, subjective ratings from the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), eye-tracking measures including gaze behavior and pupillary dynamics, and prefrontal cortical activation measured with functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Prosthesis use increased NASA-TLX mental demand by 2.80–3.85 points across tasks (all p < 0.001) and prefrontal oxygenated hemoglobin by 0.96–1.14 μ M across regions during carton transfer and pour (all p < 0.001). Pupillary activity differentiated conditions during block transfer ( p < 0.001) and checker transfer ( p < 0.05), but not carton transfer and pour ( p = 0.47), demonstrating task-dependent responses across modalities. A multimodal framework provides a more comprehensive assessment of cognitive load than any single measure alone, offering valuable insights into how cognitive demand manifests across behavioral, perceptual, and biological domains. This framework establishes a controlled baseline for multimodal cognitive workload assessment and provides a foundation for future investigations in individuals with limb loss.

items.title: Multimodal situation awareness for big data environments via adaptive sampling and dual self-distillation
items.abstract: Situation awareness (SA) in disaster management requires robust modeling of multimodal big data from complex environments. With the increasing availability of large-scale video and audio data from surveillance systems, drones, and public sensors, multimodal approaches have become essential for improving reliability. However, existing methods often rely on uniform data sampling and treat modalities equally, limiting their effectiveness when data quality varies across time and modality. Compared with our previous work, this study extends from modality-specific analysis to a multimodal audio–visual framework. To address these challenges, this paper proposes MSA-SD², a multimodal situation awareness framework specifically designed for big data environments based on selective dual self-distillation. An adaptive temporal sampling and alignment module is introduced to prioritize informative temporal segments and ensure consistent audio–visual correspondence, enabling efficient processing of large-scale multimodal big data. For visual representation, a superpixels-guided vision transformer is employed, while a transformer-based audio encoder models temporal acoustic patterns. A multimodal student model is guided by visual and audio teacher models through a selective distillation strategy that adapts to modality reliability. Experimental results demonstrate improved performance on large-scale multimodal datasets, particularly under challenging big data conditions with varying data quality across modalities.

items.title: NL2RCtrl: Risk-Controlled Controller Synthesis from Natural Language Requirements
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the translation of natural language (NL) requirements into linear temporal logic (LTL) specifications, facilitating controller synthesis for cyber-physical systems (CPSs). However, the reliability of such translations remains a concern in safety-critical applications, particularly when NL requirements are ambiguous. This paper proposes a framework based on Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to provide a statistical guarantee on the risk of issuing a controller that violates the user's intended requirement. Rather than requiring semantic equivalence between the generated and intended specifications, the proposed approach considers language inclusion, a sufficient condition for ensuring that the traces of a controller synthesized for the generated specification satisfy the intended requirement. To account for ambiguity, the LLM is queried multiple times, and the resulting LTL specifications are grouped into semantic equivalence classes and ranked by their frequency of occurrence. Given a prescribed risk level, CRC selects how many of the top-ranked equivalence classes to combine into a single LTL specification, such that the probability of issuing a controller that violates the intended requirement is bounded by that level. A controller is then synthesized for the resulting specification, or the framework abstains. Experiments on a vehicle navigation case study evaluate the proposed approach.

items.title: Occupational dust and noise exposure and worker health in the non-ferrous metal mining and processing industry in Guangxi, China, 2021–2025
items.abstract: Background Occupational hazards remain a substantial concern in the non-ferrous metal mining and processing industry. Using Guangxi’s abundant non-ferrous mineral resources, this study analyzed workplace occupational-hazard monitoring and occupational health examination data to support evidence-based prevention and control of occupational diseases in the region. Methods Using data from the monitoring system for 2021–2025, we conducted descriptive analyses of workplace occupational hazards and applied multivariable logistic regression models to identify factors associated with workers’ abnormal pulmonary function and high-frequency hearing loss. Results Between 2021 and 2025, a total of 306 enterprises and 2,379 positions were monitored. Noise showed the highest cumulative exceedance rate (33.1%), followed by dust (11.7%; C TWA exceedance of 20.0% for silica dust versus 1.2% for other dust) and lead (1.3%). Over the five-year period, workers’ exposure rates to all hazardous agents declined consistently (all p for trend < 0.001), and the silica dust exceedance rate also decreased. Among 16,213 examined workers (mean age 43.5 years; 83.2% male), the detection rate of abnormal pulmonary function was 8.7% and that of high-frequency hearing loss was 18.8%; the detection rate of hearing loss increased progressively over the years before declining in 2025. Multivariable logistic regression showed that male sex and older age were associated with both outcomes. Workers in state-owned and private enterprises had higher odds of abnormal pulmonary function (OR = 2.20 and 2.61, respectively), and the odds increased with enterprise size (OR = 1.77–2.48). For high-frequency hearing loss, workers with ≥10 years of service (OR = 1.15) and those employed in rock drilling, transportation, and flotation positions had significantly elevated odds (OR = 4.71, 2.81, and 1.91, respectively). Conclusion Supervision of noise and dust must be continuously strengthened, particularly in micro-enterprises. Optimizing engineering controls and raising awareness of personal protection are essential for reducing the risk of occupational diseases.

items.title: Occupational Hazards and Personal Protective Equipment Interventions Relevant to Environmental Health Practitioners in Government Regulatory Services: A Systematic Review of Direct and Indirect Evidence
items.abstract: Environmental Health Practitioners (EHPs) undertake regulatory, inspection and field-based activities that may expose them to multiple occupational hazards. Although personal protective equipment (PPE) is an important occupational risk-control measure, evidence concerning its effectiveness specifically among EHPs remains limited. The study aims to synthesise and evaluate available evidence on occupational hazards and the effectiveness of PPE interventions relevant to EHPs working in government regulatory services. A systematic review was conducted and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Various Research platforms were searched for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2000 and March 2026. Studies involving EHPs and related regulatory professionals were included, together with relevant evidence from comparable occupational groups where the hazards, exposure pathways or PPE interventions applied to environmental health practice. Due to heterogeneity in study designs, populations, PPE interventions and outcomes, findings were synthesised narratively. Thirty-four unique studies were included. Biological hazards were most frequently reported (82.4%), followed by chemical (47.1%), physical (44.1%), psychosocial (32.4%), organisational/workplace (26.5%), climate/environmental (17.6%) and radiation hazards (2.9%). Respiratory protection was the most frequently reported PPE category (70.6%), followed by gloves (55.9%), protective clothing (41.2%), eye/face protection (35.3%) and protective footwear (20.6%). Overall, appropriately selected PPE reduced occupational exposure; however, effectiveness varied by PPE type and occupational context and was influenced by availability, training, knowledge, adherence, comfort, correct donning and doffing, contamination control, and organisational support. Of the 34 studies, only three directly investigated EHPs, Environmental Health Officers, or Public Health Inspectors. PPE is an important component of occupational protection for EHPs but should be selected according to the specific hazard, task and exposure route and implemented within a broader occupational risk-management approach. The limited direct evidence among environmental health regulatory professionals highlights the need for EHP-specific research to inform PPE guidelines, training and occupational health policies.

items.title: On the Role of Boundary Objects in Agentic Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence involve deploying agents that execute tasks and coordinate with one another to produce outputs. These agents, to an extent, mimic human behavior in terms of the need for coordination, in which the output of one agent is used by other agents. The use of agentic AI further underscores the need to verify each agent and their interim outputs to build trustworthiness and ensure reliable final outputs. When agentic AI is used to foster human agency, the output must also be structured to enable desirable, actionable outcomes. In relation to these three areas, the use of artifacts plays an important role, as they can manifest and communicate outputs in a comprehensible manner. These artifacts serve as boundary objects, facilitating knowledge integration and the creation of a common understanding among agents and humans. Boundary object theory can therefore provide a useful lens for understanding agent-to-agent interactions, agent-to-human interactions, and, finally, human-to-human interactions based on the agents’ outputs. In this paper, we present a boundary object perspective that sheds light on facilitating interactions within both technical and sociotechnical systems. We leverage previous research on circular ecosystems to contextualize our discussion, contribute to both agentic AI and boundary object theory, and provide novel insights into the implications of transdisciplinary engineering for the use of agentic AI in complex sociotechnical systems.

items.title: Open-fMIND: A Large-Scale Open-Access fMRI Corpus for Pretraining Brain Foundation Models
items.abstract: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its application to functional MRI (fMRI) is constrained by data access. The largest standardized fMRI resources are governed by data use agreements and dominated by a small number of acquisition protocols, while the thousands of openly licensed datasets on OpenNeuro are individually small, heterogeneously organized, and unprocessed. We present the first release of Open-fMIND, a uniformly preprocessed, openly accessible corpus of parcellated fMRI timeseries from 322 OpenNeuro studies, comprising 11,379 subjects and 45,731 functional runs. Each run is preprocessed with fMRIPrep and parcellated under 52 atlases spanning 14 families, yielding a massive 2.4 million timeseries. Timeseries are released either denoised with our default pipeline (preproc) or as the fMRIPrep output with its confound files (quasiraw), with functional connectivity matrices, per-run provenance and motion metadata. Open-fMIND is intended as a pretraining resource for self-supervised brain representation learning. Pretraining on it yields downstream performance comparable to that obtained with UK Biobank.

items.title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.

items.title: Optimizing Query Decomposition for Reliable Validation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made querying databases more accessible, but cannot guarantee that the SQL they generate is correct. Without a trusted reference query, a validator (human or LLM) must decide whether a generated query answers the intended question. Enterprise questions often require queries with multiple joins, nested subqueries, and multi-level aggregation, and validating such a query in one judgment is error-prone. Decomposition simplifies this task by rewriting a query into smaller queries (blocks) that recompose to the original, each checked against its own sub-question. Decompositions differ, however: smaller blocks make each judgment easier but require more judgments, and the best balance depends on the validator's ability. We formulate validation-aware query decomposition as an optimization problem. Just as a query optimizer chooses among equivalent plans by estimated cost, we choose among decompositions by how reliably a given validator is expected to check them. We model how task difficulty and validator ability jointly affect reliability and define an objective that balances reliability against the number of judgments. Over a space of decompositions derived from logical-plan rewrites, our search finds an optimal one. We implement it in DecoVal, a pipeline that presents each block with its sub-question and input interface, combines local verdicts into a query-level decision, and localizes errors to blocks. A user study shows that decomposition helps human validators catch and locate errors: with DecoVal, participants caught 91% of the errors, up from 36% without decomposition, and located the error in nearly every rejection. Experiments on BEAVER and Spider 2.0 with LLM validators show that DecoVal also raises error-detection recall over whole-query validation while keeping precision high, and that the best granularity depends on the validator.

items.title: Pathwise-Budgeted LLM Routing: Online Allocation with K-Bit Tail-Cost Learning
items.abstract: Firms using large language models under fixed budgets must decide which model to call and whether to retry a failed task. Because a call's charge is revealed only after completion, one long response can exhaust the remaining budget and leave later tasks unserved. Our objective is to maximize the number of tasks solved before service stops. We develop a contextual bandit policy, ADP-HT, which learns each model's task-specific success probability and constructs conservative cost estimates from coarsened response-length labels on a quantile grid with $2^K$ intervals. The policy weighs predicted success against these costs, adjusting the cost penalty to realized spending and the budget available per remaining task. Under calibration, local regularity, and grid-coverage conditions, we bound the excess allowance in the policy's conservative cost estimates. At a fixed sample size, increasing $K$ reduces the discretization term but increases the estimation allowance. At the tightest tested budgets, ADP-HT solves more than twice as many MATH500 and GPQA tasks as the best implemented baseline. It achieves the highest mean cumulative score at ten of fourteen RouterBench budgets. On LiveCodeBench, it outperforms a deployed commercial router in both default and cost-saving modes at the three lowest test budgets.

items.title: Pedagogical Guidance for the Self-Realisation of High School Students in Extracurricular Activities
items.abstract: Aim. To consider how the features of pedagogical support for extracurricular activities influence the conditions and manifestations of self-realisation of high school students, as well as to establish the relationship between the nature of the environment and key indicators of self-realisation of students.Methodology. The study used a quantitative questionnaire. The survey involved 206 high school students involved in school – based education, and 203 in out-of-school extracurricular providers. Descriptive statistics and comparative analysis were used to identify differences in the perceptions of high school students’ self-actualisation support and the conditions for its implementation in extracurricular activities.Results. It is shown that the specific features of pedagogical support directly influence the conditions and manifestations of self-realisation – key determinants include the subject-subject nature of interaction with adults, support for autonomy and initiative, and developmental feedback. A stable relationship was identified between the characteristics of the organisational environment and key indicators of self-realisation. In out-of-school extracurricular providers, where voluntary participation and a horizontal interaction structure prevail, high school students demonstrate a significantly higher level of agency, self-organisation, critical thinking, and activity satisfaction, while the impact on self-awareness and career self-determination is deeper and more deliberate. In the school environment, oriented toward formal control and academic requirements, self-realisation more often retains a situational character, and the space for equitable dialogue and support of personal initiatives remains limited. The obtained data confirm that it is precisely the quality of pedagogical support and the type of educational environment that determine the depth and sustainability of self-realisation processes among high school students in extracurricular activities.Scientific novelty and research implications. The scientific novelty of this study lies in several key aspects. Firstly, it empirically establishes that the nature of pedagogical guidance (namely subject-to-subject interaction, autonomy support, and developmental feedback), rather than the mere formal availability of opportunities, serves as a crucial condition for the depth and sustainability of high school students’ self-realisation. Secondly, a robust correlation was identified between the type of organisational environment and key self-realisation metrics: voluntary and horizontal structures in extracurricular organisations statistically correlate with significantly higher levels of agency, self-awareness, and career self-determination compared to formalised school environments. Thirdly, the study proposes an operationalisation of self-realisation in extracurricular activities through a system of measurable indicators linking the quality of pedagogical interaction with students' personal outcomes. The theoretical significance consists in clarifying of the “self-realisation” concept through the prism of intrinsic motivation, as well as in demonstrating the differentiated potential of two key institutions – schools and out-of-school extracurricular providers – in creating conditions for genuine rather than situational self-realisation. The practical significance of the results lies in the possibility of using them to improve the practices of pedagogical support in schools: the transition from directive control to partner mentoring, the development of teachers’ competencies in the field of facilitation and tutoring, as well as the integration of school and out-of-school extracurricular providers resources.Conclusions. 1. A comparison of models revealed that the effectiveness of pedagogical support depends less on the type of institution and more on the nature of interaction, specifically through supporting student autonomy and initiative within a subject-subject communication framework. 2. High school students’ self-realization (manifested in agency, self-organisation, and critical thinking) is significantly associated with voluntary participation and the provision of developmental feedback. 3. The impact of extracurricular activities on self-awareness and career self-determination is strengthened by integrating reflective practices and providing opportunities for students to implement personal initiatives. 4. Satisfaction with activities correlates with the quality of pedagogical interaction, with key facilitating factors being intrinsic motivation, equitable dialogue, and a trusting environment. 5. Enhancing school-based practices is best achieved by integrating effective approaches, including developing teachers’ tutoring competencies, increasing format flexibility, and fostering network collaboration with out-of-school extracurricular providers.

items.abstract: The use of learning media is an integral component in the instructional design of Islamic Religious Education (IRE) to bridge abstract concepts into concrete ones and create a joyful learning environment. However, its implementation still faces obstacles, such as teachers' limited digital literacy, uneven school infrastructure, administrative burdens, and challenges in visualizing theological materials without diminishing the sacredness of religious teachings. This study examines the concepts, problems, impacts, and optimization strategies of media in IRE instruction. The findings indicate that the use of varied and interactive media significantly impacts students' interest, intrinsic motivation, and active participation. Key solutions to overcome these challenges include continuous professional development for digital competence, flexibility in infrastructure utilization, the implementation of educational gamification approaches, and strict content curation to maintain the accuracy of religious substances.

items.title: Perspective Chapter: Designing for Life Beyond Earth – From Ergonomic Gloves to Living Regolith: A Human-Centred Framework for Mars: Ergonomics, Materials and Well-Being Across Three Original Design Case Studies for Mars Habitability
items.abstract: Discussions of Mars exploration have long been dominated by propulsion, trajectory, and payload. Yet the most complex system in any deep-space mission is neither the rocket nor the habitat structure: it is the human being inside it. This chapter argues that design – understood in its fullest sense, from ergonomics and environmental psychology to participatory and systems-level human-centred approaches – must be repositioned as a first-order engineering and policy concern, not an afterthought applied once structural decisions have been made. This chapter examines how design thinking, human factors, and habitability science must evolve to support sustained human presence on Mars. This work explains how the role of designers is fundamental within an interdisciplinary team in which different skills intersect and complement one another. This is illustrated through three original design research projects, reviewed and presented at international conferences: a bio-based printable construction material, a 4D self-assembling shelter, and a haptic wearable device for augmented perception, thereby arguing that human-centred design, ergonomics, and astronaut well-being must be repositioned as first-order constraints in Mars mission architecture.

items.title: PharmacoMicrobiology and PharmacoMicrobioResistance: Expanding the Paradigm of Drug-Microbe Interactions and Resistance Beyond Antimicrobials in the Pharmacosphere
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is framed as a defining global health crisis, yet its conceptual boundaries remain artificially narrow. By focusing primarily on antibiotics, current paradigms ignore a broader reality: microorganisms continuously respond to the full spectrum of human and animal pharmaceuticals in both patients and the environment. This oversight obscures critical dimensions of drug action and resistance mechanisms. We propose PharmacoMicrobiology (PM) and PharmacoMicrobioResistance (PMR) to redefine microbial–drug interactions beyond traditional antimicrobials, specifically accounting for multiple simultaneous drug exposures. Microbes actively transform, degrade, and resist diverse non-antibiotic drugs, potentially undermining therapeutic efficacy across multiple distinct medical fields. Shaped by environmental contamination, microbiome dynamics, and horizontal gene transfer, resistance to these non-antibiotic drugs may already be emerging entirely unnoticed. Ignoring this expanded resistome risks repeating past failures. Integrating PM and PMR into comprehensive One Health frameworks, powered by advanced artificial intelligence, is essential to anticipate, detect, and prevent drug resistance.

items.title: Physicians Assign Themselves More Responsibility Than the General Population when AI Fails in Healthcare: A Swedish Cross-Sectional Survey
items.abstract: Background: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into clinical decision-making creates uncertainty regarding responsibility and accountability when adverse outcomes occur. Despite this, data regarding stakeholder perspectives remain scarce, especially quantitative data comparing physician and public views on responsibility allocation and transparency. This study aims to evaluate and compare how physicians and the general population in Sweden attribute responsibility for negative medical outcomes when AI is used to support healthcare decisions in primary care, as well as their views on the necessity of transparently disclosing AI use to patients.Methods: A nationwide, cross-sectional, mixed-methods survey was conducted in Sweden between February and May 2025. The survey targeted two distinct cohorts (N = 500 per group): licensed physicians under 70 years, sampled from the National Board of Health and Welfare register, and adults aged 18 or older sampled from the Swedish population registry. The survey used case vignettes as background for multiple-choice questions, with complementary open-ended free-text responses. The data was evaluated using comparative statistical analysis and reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Physicians were significantly more likely than the general population to assign responsibility to the physician (92\% vs. 74\%) and to favor a shared responsibility model involving the physician (48\% vs. 35\%). In contrast, the general population more frequently selected non-physician actor combinations (26\% vs. 8\%) and assigned greater responsibility to the patient in a scenario involving direct patient-AI interaction without a physician involved. Neither group broadly assigned responsibility to the AI itself (1.3\% physicians vs. 10\% general population). The reflexive thematic analysis reinforced these results, identifying a shared accountability framework where all actors share responsibility, but where the physician serves as the ultimate safeguard. A majority of the general population (68\%) affirmed the patient's right to always know if AI was used, in contrast to only 23\% of physicians who exhibited a polarised distribution. Conclusion: Respondents endorse a shared responsibility model among actors involved in implementing and using AI for medical decisions. The physician is viewed as the essential human-in-the-loop, bearing ultimate accountability for adverse outcomes of AI-assisted medical decisions according to a vast majority of respondents. Divergent perspectives regarding transparency emphasise the need to clarify informed consent standards for AI deployment in healthcare.

items.title: PixelBench: Evaluating Language Models for Pixel-Art Creation
items.abstract: Pixel art is widely used in games and digital content creation, requiring readable forms, coherent spatial relationships, and harmonious colors under limited resolution and palette constraints. Language models show growing promise in visual creation, yet their pixel art creation capabilities lack systematic evaluation. We introduce PixelBench, formalizing text-to-image generation and instruction-guided editing for pixel art and providing a benchmark for these tasks. We further present a creation environment in which language model agents invoke drawing tools through code to generate and edit pixel art. We assess the quality of generated artwork through human evaluation and employ a multimodal large language model as a judge, validating the agreement between its automated assessments and human preferences. We compare language models and configurations across diverse subjects and canvas sizes. In our experiments, GPT-6 Astra achieves both the highest average judge score and the best average human rank, highlighting the potential of general-purpose language models for pixel art creation. We release the tasks, all artworks, the human rankings, and the judge protocol.

items.title: Practices of Human-AI Collaboration in Enterprise Generative AI Adoption and Their Implications for Organisational Digital Innovation
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is beginning to be used in enterprise workflows as a flexible generator of text, code, images, summaries, and conversations. However, the organisation's value is not derived from technology alone. This conceptual paper explores how enterprises can organise human-AI collaboration during the adoption process and what such practices may achieve for digital innovation. Differentiate among support, sequential co-creation, iterative co-creation and supervised delegation; link these models to workflow redesign, knowledge sharing, service improvement and innovation capabilities. Based on the above discussion, the conditions for converting model outputs into responsible organisational behaviour are task decomposition, verification, role clarity, learning routines and governance. It will also solve hallucination, bias, confidentiality, deskilling, over-reliance and unequal participation. No original data, field research, experiments or performance tests were conducted. Therefore, this paper provides mechanisms and practice-oriented suggestions instead of causal results. It believes that generative AI should be treated as a fallible organisational participant in sociotechnical arrangements, and people are responsible for the goals, contextual judgement, verification and consequential decisions.

items.title: PRELIMINARY ERGONOMIC ANALYSIS OF HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS’ WORKING CONDITIONS IN A BRAZILIAN UNIVERSITY HOSPITAL EMERGENCY UNIT
items.abstract: This study analyzed the working conditions of healthcare professionals in the emergency and urgency unit of a Brazilian University Hospital using a preliminary ergonomic analysis. The method comprised two tools: the Ergonomic Checklist and the Self-Assessment Tool Ergonomics/Human Factors questionnaire. These instruments facilitated the assessment of physical, cognitive, and organizational demands within the occupational environment. The findings highlighted critical ergonomic issues, such as inadequate furniture, excessive noise, and poor lighting conditions. A high level of physical strain was noted due to the intense work pace and constant movement required, while cognitive demands were marked by time pressure, mental overload, and emotional stress. Organizational deficiencies, particularly those related to communication, were also identified as factors compromising task execution and workplace safety. The study underscores the need for ergonomic interventions, including workload adjustments, planned breaks, environmental adaptations, psychological support programs, and improved internal communication strategies. These measures aim to reduce physical and cognitive strain, promote healthier and safer working conditions, and improve the quality of patient care. Moreover, the proposed method can be systematically applied to other hospital units to determine whether the identified demands are specific to the studied unit or indicative of broader systemic challenges within the hospital environment.

items.title: Premise Recovery in Software Design: What Does This Decision Rest On?
items.abstract: Design decisions shape software architecture, and writing them down preserves the reasons behind it. Architecture decision records (ADRs) capture them, each with its context, choice, and consequences. A decision can depend on earlier ones: reversing one of them would force its review. We call these its premises. Yet ADRs do not always name their premises. When a decision is reversed, engineers supersede its ADR and search by hand for what it affects. That search can miss ADRs resting on an unnamed premise. We frame this as premise recovery: given an ADR with identifiers masked, find its premises among earlier records. We collect 1,060 ADRs from 36 repositories and label 1,529 candidate pairs for 60 target ADRs. Two LLM annotators agree at \k{appa} = 0.859. An independent human annotator, blind to their labels, agrees with the stated/implicit tag on 30 of 32 premises (\k{appa} = 0.875). We compare 7 open-weight models with 2 baselines that use no LLM. Qwen3.8-27B reaches F1 0.756, against 0.466 for word overlap; 2 models added post hoc score similarly. On the 11 premises whose titles barely overlap the target, it finds 0.758, while word overlap finds none. Reasoning raises its recall of implicit premises but not its F1. Word overlap with as many predictions gains 69% as much. We find only 2 to 3 stale dependents, though we searched for unlinked ones in only 30 of 66 supersessions. Open models could thus suggest unwritten premises when a decision is reversed, with precision between 0.68 and 0.78.

items.title: Preparing Students for the Realities of Contemporary Nursing Requires More Than Teaching Communication Models or Human-Factors Theory
items.abstract: Preparing students for the realities of contemporary nursing requires more than teaching communication models or human-factors theory. It demands learning experiences that reveal how individuals behave under pressure, ambiguity, and cognitive strain. This presentation showcases “Party Quirks”, an improvisation-based simulation that creates a controlled but deliberately chaotic environment in which students experience the emotional and behavioural challenges associated with real clinical practice. Unlike high-fidelity clinical simulation, this activity uses social unpredictability as its realism. Students must navigate unclear communication, disruptive behaviours, conflicting cues, and rising frustration while working collaboratively to solve a shared problem. These features reflect well-documented contributors to human error in healthcare such as hierarchical inhibition, task fixation, reluctance to escalate concerns, and the cognitive overload described in patient safety literature (NHS Patient Safety Strategy, 2019; Reason, 2000). The design mirrors the uncertainty and mental load that nurses routinely encounter, from unexpected interruptions to ambiguous team communication. Across multiple cohorts, “Party Quirks” has produced high engagement, rich reflective discussion, and immediate behavioural insight. Students consistently report recognising their own tendencies under pressure, including avoidance of help-seeking, overanalysis, communication breakdowns, and emotional reactions they had not anticipated. These reflections closely echo the human-factors themes explored in clinical incident analysis and safety training. The structured debrief links students’ in-game behaviours to real-world scenarios, promoting discussion around psychological safety, speaking up, situational awareness, emotional intelligence, and team dynamics. The activity has also demonstrated inclusivity benefits, offering a low-stakes, culturally flexible space in which diverse learners contribute meaningfully to teamwork and communication tasks. This session will present the design, theoretical rationale, implementation guidance, and observed outcomes of “Party Quirks”. It argues that low-resource, high-impact gamified simulations can meaningfully enhance the preparedness of nursing, midwifery, and allied health students by allowing them to feel and examine the human factors that shape safe clinical practice.
