items.title: Progressive Layer-wise Supervision: Deep-to-Shallow Supervision Annealing for Efficient and Robust Speech Deepfake Detection
items.abstract: Speech foundation models pretrained via self-supervised learning provide powerful representations for deepfake detection, yet we find that standard fine-tuning exploits only the deepest transformer layers-leaving the majority of the network's capacity discriminatively inert. Layer-wise probing of XLS-R-128 reveals that the top two-thirds of the transformer stack contribute negligibly to anti-spoofing performance after standard fine-tuning, a phenomenon we term shallow-layer dormancy. We connect this observation to the representational redundancy of pretrained transformers: adjacent layers encode highly similar information, and fine-tuning without explicit intermediate supervision reinforces rather than breaks this redundancy. To address this, we propose Progressive Layer-wise Supervision (PLS), a training framework that attaches a shared linear classifier to every transformer layer and schedules layer-wise loss contributions via an exponentially annealed power weighting. Early training concentrates supervision on deep layers to preserve the pretrained representational hierarchy; later training progressively redistributes supervision to shallower layers, converting dormant earlier representations into discriminative ones. Competitive detection (<9.25% average EER) is achievable on XLS-R-128 at layer 7, which reduces the parameter count from 315M to 101M and exemplifies an early exit mechanism. Experiments across twelve benchmarks spanning in-domain, and out-of-domain deepfake scenarios show PLS achieves a new state-of-the-art with 239M parameters, outperforming prior methods with larger and more complex architectures.

items.title: PromptPoseFX: Authoring Pose-Driven Visual Effects through Augmented Prompting and Interactive Refinement
items.abstract: Human pose-driven visual effects offer a compelling way for enhancing video expressiveness and storytelling. Authoring such effects with traditional video editing tools is a complex and time-consuming task that requires considerable technical expertise and manual effort. While generative AI models can simplify the workflow by reducing manual scripting through language-driven generation, existing approaches suffer from imprecise alignment between visual effects and pose data, failure to preserve original video content, and limited support for fine-grained, iterative refinement. To address these challenges, we present PromptPoseFX, an interactive system that allows creators to author pose-driven visual effects through augmented language prompts and interactive refinement. Our system leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to translate high-level user intent into parameterized procedural graphics scripts, automatically mapping pose-tracking data to specific effect parameters, allowing precise alignment with human motion. This script-based approach manages effects as independent layers, thereby preserving the original content of the underlying video. To reduce language ambiguity, our interface offers controls across spatial, temporal, and parameter domains, enabling the precise, intuitive, and iterative authoring of pose-driven visual effects. We evaluated PromptPoseFX through a comparative study against a text-only LLM interface, followed by an exploratory study. In the comparative study, participants rated PromptPoseFX significantly higher than the text-only baseline on measures of perceived control and precision. The exploratory study examined usability and creativity support in open-ended authoring tasks.

items.title: Proposed new words and collective identity in human and language model agent groups
items.abstract: Groups develop distinctive words even when ordinary expressions are sufficient. Such words can symbolize collective identity, and observational studies link language use to community attachment. We examined identity change in temporary groups of one human and four disclosed large language model (LLM) agents, comparing discussions with and without a neologism proposal across recruitment waves. We recruited 100 Japanese participants in two sequential waves; an agent proposed a new word only in the first wave. Mean collective identity change did not differ significantly between waves. Within the proposal wave, favorable ratings of the proposed word were associated with change in identity, but this association did not survive correction for multiple testing (adjusted $$p=0.229$$ ). The three-way interaction among recruitment wave, message count, and team impression had a nominal $$p=0.027$$ but did not survive correction (adjusted $$p=0.082$$ ). In a sensitivity analysis, the interaction was not significant after adjustment for midpoint identity (nominal $$p=0.078$$ ; adjusted $$p=0.624$$ ). The nonsignificant between-wave comparison and exploratory associations that did not survive correction, together with wave confounding and post-discussion evaluations, limit causal inference and motivate randomized studies with repeated measures to test whether proposed group language affects identification.

items.title: PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGICAL DEVELOPMENT CHARACTERISTICS OF PRIMARY SCHOOL STUDENTS AND THE ROLE OF PLAY ACTIVITIES IN ENHANCING THEIR COGNITIVE ENGAGEMENT
items.abstract: The psychophysiological development of primary school children is fundamental for their academic success, yet the systematic integration of play to enhance cognitive engagement, especially its specific mechanisms, remains understudied. The aim of this study is to investigate primary school children's psychophysiological development and play's role in enhancing cognitive engagement. This article explores the intricate link between psychophysiological maturation—including brain development, motor skills, sensory processing, and emotional regulation—and cognitive engagement. It examines how these developmental trajectories influence learning and how play-based strategies can bridge developmental gaps. The text highlights that rapid brain development, particularly in the prefrontal cortex, enhances executive functions, inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility. It emphasizes that myelination improves neural transmission, while refined motor and sensory skills, alongside evolving emotional regulation, are crucial for sustained attention and active participation. items.title: Reading Royalty Risk at Scale: LLM-Assisted Construction and Reliability Analysis of an Offset- and-Deduction Clause Corpus from SEC-Filed Technology Licences
items.abstract: We introduce RODEO , a corpus of 5,111 royalty offset and deduction clause spans from material-contract exhibits filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (709 exhibits, 417 filers), labelled for their economic function under a seven-function taxonomy. Because exhaustive human annotation is costly, we build the resource with a protocol assisted by a large language model (LLM): independent double classification, adjudication of substantive disagreements, and a stratified human spot-check. We release the corpus with source identifiers and privacy-screened excerpts, together with the per-pass and adjudicated labels, prompts and code. As a quality-control analysis we examine how far the model can be trusted. It is highly self-consistent on the surface (82.4% exact-set agreement across passes) yet poorly calibrated: 82% of predictions carry the maximal confidence score, even that top bin flips label across passes 13.8% of the time, and the model’s own uncertainty flag recovers only 1% of genuine disagreements. On a deliberately hard subset, a model from an independent family agrees with the adjudicated label only 36.6% of the time, whereas on a broad stratified sample the two LLM annotators agree substantially (macro Cohen’s κ = 0.78). Inter-pass disagreement, not self-reported confidence, is therefore the more useful signal for triaging hard cases when full human labelling is infeasible. Supervised baselines show that the labelling is learnable (a bag-of-words logistic-regression classifier reaches macro-F1 0.80; the notice-and-documentation condition is hardest). The released labels are LLM-generated with a human spot-check (“silver”), and we set out the path to a fully human-adjudicated version.

items.title: REEL: Brain-Guided Video Generation and Selection by Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear Decoding from fMRI data
items.abstract: Visual brain decoding from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data has made remarkable progress in recent years, driven by increasingly powerful artificial intelligence (AI) models and the growing availability of large-scale public datasets. However, despite the impressive advances achieved in static image decoding, the reconstruction of videos from fMRI signals remains challenging due to the temporal mismatch between rapidly changing video stimuli and the slow dynamics of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response. We evaluate a Bayesian-inspired proposal-and-rerank strategy on CC2017 and the BOLD Moments Dataset (BMD), using a linear semantic decoder, a pretrained video generator, and three neural encoding streams with ridge readouts and learned pooling in two streams. We refer to this framework as REEL (Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear decoding). Compared with a single generated candidate, reranking increases mean Video 50-way accuracy from 0.2359 to 0.2434 across three CC2017 participants and from 0.3653 to 0.3920 across ten BMD participants. These findings suggest an alternative and conceptually simpler strategy for improving video brain decoding, highlighting the potential of our approach as a complementary direction to increasingly complex pipelines.

items.title: Reflective, Experiential and Coaching-Based Workplace Learning in Service Organisations A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Service organisations depend on frontline employees whose competence is built largely at work, yet evidence on structured workplace learning remains fragmented. This systematic literature review synthesises empirical evidence on reflective, experiential and coaching-based learning among in-service workers and identifies the organisational conditions that shape it. Following PRISMA 2020, 97 open-access journal articles published between 2021 and 2026 were retrieved from Scopus and screened against set eligibility criteria. Twenty-nine studies were included, appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and synthesised thematically. The evidence was dominated by healthcare and human services in high-income countries, qualitative designs and self-reported outcomes. Five themes emerged, (1) reflection works best when built into daily work; (2) real work experience builds skills when it matches the job; (3) coaching and feedback depend on prepared coaches and trust; (4) peers and groups spread new practice across teams; and (5) workplace conditions, such as supervisor support, psychological safety, hierarchy and workload, decide whether learning is used. The review proposes a structured workplace learning cycle linking these elements. Workplace learning becomes sustainable when it is built into daily work and supported by supervisors. Stronger behavioural evidence is needed from Southeast Asian and frontline service sectors such as private security.

items.title: Relación de la ergonomía con la calidad de vida del docente universitario
items.abstract: Introduction: University professors, immersed in demanding and highly technologized work environments, face conditions that compromise their physical, cognitive, emotional, and social well-being. In this context, ergonomics emerges as a key discipline to mitigate disergonomic risks and foster healthy work environments. Objective: Characterize the relationship between ergonomic factors (physical, cognitive, organizational, and environmental) and the quality of life of university professors, based on the most recent scientific evidence. Methods: An integrative review of scientific literature published between 2019 and 2024 was conducted in the databases Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, SciELO, and Redalyc. Search strategies combined Boolean operators (“ergonom*” AND “university professor” AND “quality of life”) with equivalent MeSH and DeCS terms. Eligible documents included peer-reviewed articles, empirical studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses. Inclusion criteria considered thematic relevance, methodological rigor, and full-text availability. A total of 52 studies met the inclusion criteria. Results: Ergonomic factors are closely associated with the overall well-being of university faculty. Ergonomic interventions improve musculoskeletal health, reduce cognitive fatigue, promote job satisfaction, and optimize the environmental conditions of academic work. Conclusions: Ergonomics, when addressed holistically and at the institutional level, represents a key strategy for enhancing the quality of life of university professors. Its systematic implementation fosters professional performance and helps prevent occupational diseases.

items.title: RemeshingAgent: An Iterative Agent for Repair-Based Decimation of Generated Building Meshes
items.abstract: Aggressively simplifying a generated high-poly building mesh to 0.5-1% of its faces confronts a hard limit. The surface looks complete, yet the mesh is topologically shattered: 10^3-10^4 connected components and non-manifold thin walls. Below a certain budget, every practical decimator "melts": it deletes parts, welds thin walls, or breaks the error tolerance. We attribute this to instance-specific pathology: which components are significant and where the cliff sits vary from mesh to mesh, so no single fixed algorithm suffices, and decimation becomes an iterative loop of cleaning, simplifying, and verifying. We present RemeshingAgent, an agent that turns this loop into a validated process. The melting follows from a triangle-budget decomposition into curvature, crease, component, and genus terms: below the component floor, no output satisfies the repair contract, and cleaning first is the theory-mandated response. At a 0.5% budget the agent stays topology-clean where QEM and vertex clustering melt, matches a commercial remesher on 20 unseen city buildings, and on the 24 training buildings a nine-participant single-workstation blind study prefers our outputs 168:48 (p = 0.0195, subject-level sign test). The trained skill deploys as retrieval replay: 11.7 seconds per mesh on CPU, with no LLM calls.

items.title: Research on the Knowledge Transformation of Educational Discourse on Short-Video Platforms and the Cognitive Engagement Pathways of Learners
items.abstract: With the development of mobile internet, short video platforms have become important venues for knowledge dissemination and learning, significantly impacting traditional modes of educational discourse production and communication. This study takes educational discourse on short video platforms as its research subject, focusing on knowledge transformation mechanisms and learners' cognitive engagement processes. By integrating literature review, content analysis, and case studies, it comprehensively examines the patterns through which knowledge evolves from implicit to explicit and from specialized to popular within short video education contexts. Educational discourse on short video platforms is characterized by fragmentation, visuality, and interactivity. Knowledge transformation primarily occurs through discourse simplification, contextual embedding, emotional activation, and symbolic reconstruction. Creators employ narrative techniques and visual language to reduce the complexity of knowledge, making abstract concepts more accessible. Meanwhile, learners' cognitive engagement is diverse and multi-faceted, involving attention capture, information processing, meaning construction, and knowledge transfer—manifested in social behaviors such as commenting, liking, and sharing—which can either positively or negatively influence deep learning. Furthermore, there exists an interactive relationship among platform algorithms, content creators’ professionalism, and learners’ self-regulation abilities: while algorithms enhance accessibility to knowledge, they may also lead to superficial cognition and echo chambers. Based on these findings, this paper offers recommendations for improving the creation of educational content on short video platforms, including enhancing content quality and authenticity, building interactive cognitive scaffolds, and improving learners’ media literacy. These suggestions aim to provide insights and support for maximizing the educational potential of short video platforms and promoting learners’ cognitive development, thereby contributing to the healthy growth of informal learning in the digital age.

items.title: Rethinking Feature Selection: A Fair-Division Approach Under Model Uncertainty
items.abstract: Feature selection, also known as variable selection, is a foundational problem in econometrics, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. However, widely used procedures may be inaccurate, unstable under collinearity, and sensitive to sampling noise and may lack a principled interpretation in terms of how they allocate explanatory power. This paper develops a feature-selection framework that extends a fair-division approach introduced by Hu ([2020, 2025). We represent the explanatory or forecasting performance of feature subsets as payoffs in a coalitional game subject to sampling uncertainty. Candidate features are partitioned into selected and unselected sets according to their fair-division values, defined using a modified Shapley value. Model uncertainty is represented by a beta-binomial distribution over subset size and a uniform distribution over subsets conditional on size. Each feature’s value combines the expected marginal gain from inclusion with the expected opportunity loss associated with exclusion, thereby treating all candidates symmetrically ex ante under a veil-of-ignorance principle. We further propose a sequential selection algorithm that uses a Monte Carlo approximation and a likelihood-ratio screening rule that admits at most one feature per iteration. Across the simulation designs considered, the procedure attains substantially higher exact-identification rates than those of the benchmark methods, including stepwise, unidirectional, GETS-style, and LASSO-based procedures. The paper also examines residual-share-based hyperparameter calibration, computational complexity, selection consistency, and practical implementation considerations.

items.title: Rethinking Social Sustainability Metrics in Chile’s Lithium Sociotechnical Transition: Numbers, Policies and Knowledge
items.abstract: Social sustainability indicators are central decision-support tools in mining, used to evaluate social performance and guide policy and investment. However, these indicators do not merely describe reality; they actively shape it by defining what is measured, reported, and governed. In the context of lithium extraction from brines, this performative role becomes particularly relevant as expanding production and technological changes reconfigure water use, territorial relations, and community livelihoods in sensitive ecosystems such as the high-Andean salt flats of Chile, which host some of the world’s largest lithium reserves and production sites. This paper analyses how social sustainability is currently measured in the lithium industry and identifies the opportunities and limitations of existing indicator frameworks. Using a systematic analysis of sustainability reports and international reporting standards, combined with insights from stakeholder interviews, we examine the indicators commonly used to assess lithium extraction activities. The results show that existing indicator systems are structured by global reporting standards and compliance-oriented metrics, whilst territorial dynamics and relational aspects of social sustainability remain partially captured. Based on these results, the paper discusses implications for the design of social sustainability indicators in critical mineral extraction. We argue that improving sustainability assessment requires incorporating territorially situated perspectives, ecosystem-based knowledge, and broader participation of communities, universities, public institutions, and firms. In this sense, redesigning sustainability indicators as more reflexive and participatory tools may support more socially robust pathways in the sociotechnical transition of the lithium industry in Chile.

items.title: Revisiting the Survival of Agent-Attributed Code: How Measurement Choices Decide the Verdict
items.abstract: Studies of how long code from AI coding agents survives after it is merged reach conflicting verdicts: agent code is reported to be retained longer than human code, about as long, or modified sooner. Each study makes defensible measurement choices, but how much these choices decide the verdict is unknown. We revisit the survival of agent-attributed code in our earlier study: 854,139 lines that 2,802 merged pull requests (PRs) added to 215 repositories of the AIDev dataset. We vary nine measurement choices in five research questions and build a specification curve of 88 survival analyses, tested under three variance estimators, several observation windows, and permuted labels. items.title: Revisiting warranting theory in AI-mediated communication: An evaluation of writer and source effects in online reviews.
items.abstract: This article examines how attributing the actual writer of an online message to artificial intelligence (AI) , rather than a human, shapes impression formation . By drawing on and extending warranting theory, this article examines how source role labels (self vs. third party) and content writer labels (AI vs. human) interact to affect impression formation and message effects in the context of hotel reviews. Two preregistered experiments (Study 1: N = 461; Study 2: N = 444) found that, for the same positive hotel review, third-party reviewers were perceived more favorably than self-reviewers (i.e., hotel managers), leading to more positive evaluations of the hotel. Reviews attributed to AI writers negatively impacted impressions of the reviewer and diminished the review’s impact, with third-party reviewers more negatively affected by AI writer labels than self-reviewers. AI labels of user-generated content, therefore, attenuate the effects of source role and move people out of their default impression formation state. We demonstrate theoretical advancements for warranting theory and AI-mediated communication.

items.title: RFAmpDesigner: A Two-Level LLM-guided Optimization Framework for Automated Differential CMOS RF Amplifier Sizing
items.abstract: Automated RF amplifier sizing is challenging because the design process is inherently hierarchical, the parameter space is high-dimensional and strongly coupled, and high-fidelity circuit simulation is expensive. Conventional optimization and reinforcement learning methods typically require many iterations and make limited use of RF domain knowledge, making them costly under tight simulation budgets. Large language models (LLMs) provide broad prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but are unreliable for direct numerical optimization. This paper presents RFAmpDesigner, a two-level optimization framework for automated schematic-level sizing of differential CMOS RF amplifiers. At the outer level, the circuit-parameter space is abstracted into a resource-allocation space, where LLMs make high-level allocation decisions and adjust them according to feedback from the inner level. At the inner level, RF design knowledge is used to decompose the flat sizing problem into a sequence of low-dimensional subproblems. Conventional optimizers then solve these subproblems to find circuit implementations consistent with the assigned resources. This structure allows numerical optimizers to focus on low-dimensional searches in the circuit-parameter space, while the LLM reasons and acts over a physically meaningful design space using simulation feedback. The main evaluation covers low-noise amplifier (LNA), driver amplifier (DA), and power amplifier (PA) designs within the target differential CMOS RF amplifier family. Experimental results show that it achieves a higher success rate under a limited simulation budget in both easy and hard regimes.

items.title: ROBOTIC-ASSISTED SURGERY IN MODERN HEALTHCARE: CLINICAL EFFECTIVENESS, ECONOMIC ACCESSIBILITY, AND SOCIETAL IMPLICATIONS OF THE DA VINCI SURGICAL SYSTEM
items.abstract: Background: Robotic-assisted surgery has become an increasingly prominent component of modern healthcare, with the da Vinci Surgical System representing one of the most widely adopted platforms. Despite its technological advantages, including enhanced instrument articulation, three-dimensional visualization, and improved surgical ergonomics, questions remain regarding its comparative clinical effectiveness, economic accessibility, and broader implications for healthcare systems. Aim: This review critically examines the available evidence concerning the clinical outcomes and economic implications of da Vinci-assisted procedures compared with conventional laparoscopic and open surgery. Materials and Methods: Particular attention is given to operative time, postoperative complications, hospital stay, surgical conversion rates, and healthcare expenditure. The review also considers the influence of institutional resources, surgical expertise, and technological accessibility on the implementation of robotic-assisted procedures. Results: Recent comparative studies indicate that robotic surgery may offer advantages in selected surgical settings; however, these benefits are not consistently demonstrated across all procedures and patient populations. Furthermore, substantial financial requirements and methodological limitations in existing economic evaluations complicate conclusions regarding cost-effectiveness. Conclusions: The findings highlight the importance of procedure-specific evidence and balanced healthcare investment decisions. Robotic-assisted surgery should therefore be evaluated not solely as a technological innovation but as a healthcare intervention whose clinical value, affordability, and accessibility must be assessed together.

items.title: Rubric-Based AES with LLM Ensembles: Scoring of Student Responses in Critical Online Reasoning Using Ensembles of LLMs
items.abstract: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.

items.title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety
items.abstract: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Safety-Preserving Medical LLM Fine-Tuning via Bilevel Data Selection
items.abstract: As general large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted for patient-facing medical applications, improving medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks remains a critical challenge. Large-scale medical instruction data are essential for acquiring domain knowledge through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), but unsafe responses can undermine existing safety alignment. To address this problem, we propose Scalable Bilevel Data Selection (S-BDS) for safety-preserving medical SFT. By controlling selection-weight concentration, S-BDS enables reliable sample ranking over large candidate pools and identifies training examples that improve medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks. We combine clinician-validated safe data and selected data with unscreened medical instruction data for SFT, and jointly evaluate medical capability and patient-facing safety on HealthBench and PatientSafetyBench, respectively. Experiments across Llama and Qwen models show that S-BDS achieves the highest safe rates among all compared methods, outperforming the strongest baselines by 4.64 and 3.00 percentage points, respectively, while maintaining competitive medical capability. Further experiments show that varying the safety-oriented weight during SFT controls the trade-off between medical capability and patient-facing safety.

items.title: Same Papers, Different Verdicts: Tracing Version Drift in LLM Peer Review
items.abstract: Venues and benchmarks read LLM review scores as measurements of a paper, while providers replace their models within months. We audit twenty frontier models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic on ICLR 2027 submissions while they were under review, with tests registered before the decisions. Between an earlier and a later version of Claude Opus and of Gemini, the share of papers placed on the accept side falls by 52 and 53 percentage points on 183 and 60 randomly drawn submissions, and by 43 to 79 points in six further paired comparisons, with no paper moving up in any of them. Stating a 30% acceptance rate in the prompt leaves a gap of 79 points between the two Opus versions. When score-stripped critiques are swapped between versions, the later critiques alone lower the accept share by 35 points for Opus and 51 for Gemini; for Opus the drop is 35 points under a third-party scorer and 24 after a rewrite that keeps each technical point and removes evaluative wording. On 57 papers, the percentiles of Opus 4.6 and 5.5 correlate at 0.73 while their accept shares differ by 44 points. On 99 to 119 submissions, the self-estimated percentiles of three models correlate with two human reviewers more strongly than a third reviewer does (point estimates 0.17 to 0.21, 95% intervals between -0.04 and +0.42). All twenty models give a 2 or a 3 in 473 of their 475 reviews, against 60 of 72 human reviews. Retrospective tests on decided papers can draw on memory. Claude Opus 5.5 names the true first author of 27 decided ICLR 2026 papers from their titles alone, with no wrong name, and Claude Opus 4.6 accepted all 11 decided papers it said it recognized, against 5 expected. Thresholds on LLM-reviewer scores therefore have to be validated against human decisions for each model version; our tests against the ICLR 2027 decisions follow on 16 December 2026.

items.title: Scaffolded large language model feedback builds durable translation competence whereas unrestricted use fosters dependency
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly entering translator education, yet it remains unclear whether they build students' own translation competence or merely improve the products students submit. We combined a validation study on public benchmark data with a 16-week quasi-experiment to test a scaffolded human--LLM pedagogy, the Draft--Diagnose--Revise--Reflect (D2R) cycle, for English--Chinese translation. In Study 1, a rubric-guided error-annotation prompt increased the agreement between LLM feedback and expert Multidimensional Quality Metrics judgements on 2,500 WMT segments for all four models tested; with this prompt GPT-4o reached a segment-level Kendall's $\tau$ of 0.30, on a par with the strongest neural metric, and the highest error-detection accuracy. In Study 2, 179 English majors received conventional instruction, unrestricted LLM access or the guardrailed D2R cycle. Unrestricted access maximised LLM-assisted performance but yielded no advantage in unassisted translation over conventional instruction at a delayed test 12 weeks after the course (Hedges' $g$ = $-$0.08) and produced the largest AI-dependency gap. Scaffolded use produced durable gains in unassisted translation ($g$ = 0.70), a 13\% reduction in error rate and higher metacognitive regulation. Process logs indicated that the benefit was transmitted mainly through lower verbatim adoption of LLM output. Pedagogical design, not LLM access per se, determines whether LLMs support or supplant translation learning.

items.title: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters
items.abstract: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.

items.title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential route to automating scientific programming, but their usefulness depends on consistently producing numerically correct code. We extend FEM-Bench to 17 finite element tasks involving nonlinear and history-dependent mechanics and structural dynamics, and evaluate 15 models on implementation and test generation without execution feedback. The best model succeeds in 87.1% of single-pass implementation trials, but rankings differ between tracks. The leading implementer achieves 49.9% joint test success, while the leading tester reaches 82.6%. For six models, we compare single-pass generation with two agentic harnesses that allow code execution and revision. Agentic execution solves some tasks that never succeeded in single-pass trials and improves consistency on others, but gains vary across models and harnesses, and regressions also occur. Claude Opus 5 with SimpleAgent reaches 96.5% Pass@3, the probability of at least one success in three attempts, but 77.1% Pass$^3$, the probability that all three succeed. No model-harness combination exceeds 78.8% Pass$^3$. To understand why agents submit incorrect code after passing their own checks, we analyze 249 failed agentic trajectories and identify six categories of self-verification failure. The most common are inadequate test coverage (73.1%) and reliance on generic consistency checks (70.3%), and in 28.5% of cases the tests share an error with the implementation. Motivated by these findings, an exploratory configuration with separate coder and tester agents achieves the highest observed scores, with 97.6% Pass@3 and 88.8% Pass$^3$. These results identify consistency across attempts and independent verification as the main obstacles to trusting LLM-generated scientific code.

items.title: Screening and reporting of occupational noise related hearing disorders using MySmartOH—a cloud-based analytics solution
items.abstract: This study was aimed to evaluate the validity and agreement of MySmartOH (a novel cloud-based analytical software), as compared to conventional audiometric test, for screening of occupational noise–related hearing disorders (ONRHDs) among Malaysian workers. Subsequently, the time taken for screening and reporting between MySmartOH and the conventional paper-based approach was compared. This cross-sectional study involved 16 occupational health doctors and 320 audiograms. For each hearing condition, sensitivity and specificity tests were used to determine the software’s validity while Cohen’s kappa coefficient was used to assess its agreement. The time taken to screen and report ONRHDs between MySmartOH and the conventional method was analysed. The sensitivity of MySmartOH ranged from 55.6 to 99.1% while specificity ranged between 70.0 and 99.2%. Cohen’s kappa values for MySmartOH ranged between 0.41 and 0.92. For the left ear, screening and reporting were faster with MySmartOH (0.93 and 0.48 min) than with the conventional method (1.25 and 0.87 min). For the right ear, MySmartOH also shortened screening (0.87 vs. 1.15 min) and reporting times (0.47 vs. 0.83 min). MySmartOH reduced screening time by 24.3–25.6% and reporting time by 43.3–44.8%. MySmartOH demonstrated variable diagnostic performance, with moderate-to-high agreement for screening ONRHDs compared with conventional audiometric assessment. It also offers a faster alternative to the conventional method.

items.title: Scribble Once, Segment the Sequence: Bidirectional Temporal Consistency for Weakly Supervised Segmentation in Echocardiography Sequences
items.abstract: Temporal medical image segmentation relies on pixel-wise annotations, which are prohibitively expensive for long image sequences. Existing weakly-supervised methods reduce the annotation burden per frame but still require repeated annotations across the sequence. Furthermore, sparse supervision can result in temporally unstable representations. Addressing both challenges requires a model that can leverage strong spatial priors from large-scale pretraining while minimizing reliance on dense annotations. Frozen 2D vision foundation models provide a promising basis for this by offering transferable spatial representations with low trainable parameters. However, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits their ability to propagate reliable information across anatomical sequences. To address this, we present a weakly-supervised framework for temporal segmentation from a single scribble-annotated frame, with all remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of DINOv3 encoders present in the mean-teacher architecture. Furthermore, a set of complementary losses, including a temporal loss helps generate reliable segmentation priors for the unlabeled frames. This formulation decouples annotation costs from sequence length while retaining the transferable spatial knowledge of the pretrained encoder. Extensive experiments on the publicly available CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms other scribble-supervised methods. These results show that accurate and temporally consistent segmentation can be achieved from extremely sparse supervision, substantially reducing annotation requirements for temporal echocardiographic segmentation and providing a practical framework for scalable clinical deployment.

items.title: Short-term cognitive impairments during night work: a meta-analysis and systematic review
items.abstract: Cognitive performance is used as a proxy for work performance and safety. This meta -analysis and systematic review compared cognitive performance during night shifts (23:00–07:00) with daytime performance (07:00–23:00) across experimental field and laboratory studies, excluding shifts exceeding 24 h. Meta-regressions examined night shift, study context, and cognitive test characteristics as sources of heterogeneity. Fifty-five studies were included, yielding 758 night work and 964 daytime datapoints from 1,919 participants, combined into 6135 effect sizes. Cognitive performance was impaired during night shifts relative to daytime hours (Hedges g = −0.36, 95% CI [−0.49, −0.23], p < 0.001), although indications of publication bias suggest this pooled estimate is somewhat inflated. Impairments increased with time into the shift, from 0:01–08:59 h (g = −0.33, 95% CI [−0.63, −0.02], p = 0.041) to > 9 h (g = −0.61, 95% CI [−0.96, −0.25], p = 0.004). Impairments were more pronounced on simple tests (g = −0.50, 95% CI [−0.70, −0.31], p < 0.001), as complex tests weakened the night-daytime difference (g = 0.29, 95% CI [0.07, 0.50], p < 0.001). This contrast was driven by the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT); excluding PVT data removed the difference and attenuated the pooled effect to g = −0.24. No significant moderating effects emerged for time point during the shift, shift sequence, test outcome, or study context (field vs. laboratory). Extended night shifts thus appear detrimental to safety, with heightened sensitivity concentrated in psychomotor vigilance type tasks. Both contexts appear valid for examining these effects. Remaining heterogeneity warrants further investigation of environmental and individual factors.

items.title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
items.abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.

items.title: SpeCal: Spectral Calibration for Unsupervised RLVR
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning abilities of large language models, but its dependence on ground-truth answers or external verifiers limits its ability to exploit abundant unlabeled reasoning data. Unsupervised RLVR alleviates this bottleneck by deriving scalar rewards from the model's own rollouts. However, the reliability of such self-generated supervision varies substantially across rollout groups and individual responses, while existing methods construct or refine their rewards mainly from decoded outcomes and reward statistics. These endpoint signals reveal what answers the model produces, but provide limited information about whether the underlying rollout representations form a reliable structure for learning. Our key observation is that hidden-state spectra offer a complementary view of supervision reliability by characterizing both the organization of a rollout group and the support received by each rollout within that group. Based on this observation, we propose SpeCal, a bi-level spectral calibration framework for unsupervised RLVR. At the group level, SpeCal combines spectral mass with a Gaussian band-pass gate over normalized entropy-based effective rank, favoring rollout groups with substantial representation variation whose effective dimensionality lies in a preferred regime. At the rollout level, the same group effective rank determines how many dominant directions are retained in a leave-one-out spectral subspace formed by the remaining rollouts, within which the conditional support of each held-out rollout is measured. The resulting signals calibrate the original reward-induced advantages at the group and rollout levels without redefining the underlying unlabeled reward.

items.title: Strategic futures of B2B marketing: a Delphi-based foresight study on AI and interconnected drivers of transformation
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the strategic futures of business-to-business (B2B) marketing by identifying the interlinked themes shaping its transformation, with particular attention to artificial intelligence (AI) as a cross-cutting force embedded in sociotechnical and institutional developments. Design/methodology/approach A two-round Delphi study with 29C-level industry experts was conducted. Responses were coded into 192 thematic mentions across 16 themes, analyzed through co-occurrence mapping and classified in a dual-axis typology by perceived nature (opportunity vs challenge) and origin (sociotechnical vs institutional). Findings AI is central but rarely operates in isolation: it co-occurs with every other theme, functioning as the connective node between internal capabilities and external demands in interorganizational relationships. The typology reveals a statistically significant attribution asymmetry (χ2(1) = 40.23, p < 0.001): internally buildable themes are framed as opportunities, externally imposed demands as challenges. Originality/value The paper theorizes AI not as a tool within the firm but as a boundary-spanning coordination mechanism coupling sociotechnical and institutional domains. The dual-axis typology, tested attribution asymmetry and three propositions provide a foresight-driven framework for understanding strategic readiness in B2B transformation.

items.title: Structure-aware transfer of genomic foundation representations across population and cross-clade classification
items.abstract: Genomic foundation models provide transferable DNA sequence representations, but their application to sample-level classification requires effective integration of sequencing reads. We present EvoGR (Evo 2-based Genomic Representation), a read-level transfer framework using a shared frozen Evo 2 encoder and Permutation-invariant Attention Aggregation (PAA). Mean pooling converts variable-length single-stranded reads into fixed-dimensional embeddings, while PAA integrates variable-sized, unordered read sets. EvoGR addresses two complementary tasks: population classification using AIM-enriched reads and four-class genome-origin classification involving human, non-human animal, plant, and microorganism sequences. Inference requires only single-stranded reads, without reference genomes, SNP coordinates, or explicit REF/ALT representations. EvoGR achieved competitive performance across both tasks and maintained strong classification performance on real human sequencing data, demonstrating transfer from simulated to real sequencing inputs. Comparisons across genomic foundation models identified Evo 2 as the strongest encoder under the evaluated settings. Ablation experiments demonstrated the contribution of PAA, while read-length sensitivity analyses showed that longer reads generally improved classification performance, with diminishing gains at greater lengths. These findings establish EvoGR as a unified framework for read-level genomic representation transfer across distinct biological classification tasks.

items.title: Students’ engagement and perceived effectiveness of Wordwall activities for ESL sentence construction
items.abstract: This study investigated students' behavioural, emotional and cognitive engagement, and their perceived effectiveness of Wordwall, following the use of Wordwall activities in English sentence construction lessons in one secondary school in Malaysia. While digital and game-based learning are gaining traction in the language classroom, constructing sentences can be a challenge for language learners and may need to be practised multiple times with feedback and active engagement. A quantitative descriptive survey design was employed with 55 Form 1 and Form 2 students from four classes in one secondary school in Malaysia. The participants engaged in three Wordwall-based sentence construction sessions followed by a post-intervention questionnaire that measured behavioural, emotional and cognitive engagement and the perceived effectiveness of Wordwall. The data were analysed using frequencies, means, standard deviations and Cronbach's alpha to assess the internal consistency of the questionnaire scales. The results showed that self-reported engagement scores were moderately positive across all three dimensions, with emotional engagement recording the highest mean score (M = 3.45, SD = 0.85), followed by cognitive engagement (M = 3.42, SD = 0.82) and behavioural engagement (M = 3.34, SD = 0.84); however, differences among the three dimensions were small. Students also reported moderately positive perceptions of the effectiveness of Wordwall for learning sentence construction (M = 3.28, SD = 1.09). These findings suggest that Wordwall may serve as a supplementary tool in interactive and participatory sentence construction lessons. However, the study did not measure learning gains, no control group was used, and the small convenience sample limits generalisation; the results therefore reflect students' self-reported perceptions only. Future research should incorporate objective measures of learning and stronger comparative designs in ESL classrooms. Kajian ini meneliti penglibatan tingkah laku, emosi dan kognitif pelajar serta persepsi mereka terhadap keberkesanan Wordwall susulan penggunaan aktiviti Wordwall dalam pengajaran pembinaan ayat bahasa Inggeris di sebuah sekolah menengah di Malaysia. Walaupun pembelajaran digital dan pembelajaran berasaskan permainan semakin mendapat tempat dalam bilik darjah bahasa, pembinaan ayat boleh menjadi cabaran kepada pelajar dan mungkin memerlukan latihan berulang dengan maklum balas serta penglibatan aktif. Reka bentuk tinjauan deskriptif kuantitatif digunakan melibatkan 55 orang pelajar Tingkatan 1 dan Tingkatan 2 daripada empat kelas di sebuah sekolah menengah di Malaysia. Peserta kajian mengambil bahagian dalam tiga sesi pembinaan ayat berasaskan Wordwall yang diikuti dengan soal selidik pascaintervensi untuk mengukur penglibatan tingkah laku, emosi dan kognitif serta persepsi terhadap keberkesanan Wordwall. Data dianalisis menggunakan kekerapan, min, sisihan piawai dan alfa Cronbach bagi menilai ketekalan dalaman skala soal selidik tersebut. Dapatan kajian menunjukkan bahawa skor penglibatan yang dilaporkan sendiri oleh pelajar berada pada tahap sederhana positif merentasi ketiga-tiga dimensi, dengan penglibatan emosi mencatatkan skor min tertinggi (M = 3.45, SD = 0.85), diikuti oleh penglibatan kognitif (M = 3.42, SD = 0.82) dan penglibatan tingkah laku (M = 3.34, SD = 0.84). Walau bagaimanapun, perbezaan antara ketiga-tiga dimensi tersebut adalah kecil. Pelajar juga melaporkan persepsi yang sederhana positif terhadap keberkesanan Wordwall dalam pembelajaran pembinaan ayat (M = 3.28, SD = 1.09). Dapatan ini menunjukkan bahawa Wordwall berpotensi digunakan sebagai alat sokongan dalam pengajaran pembinaan ayat secara interaktif dan melibatkan penyertaan aktif pelajar. Namun demikian, kajian ini tidak mengukur peningkatan hasil pembelajaran, tiada kumpulan kawalan digunakan, dan saiz sampel mudah yang kecil membataskan kebolehumuman dapatan. Oleh itu, dapatan kajian ini hanya mencerminkan persepsi yang dilaporkan sendiri oleh pelajar. Kajian pada masa hadapan wajar menggunakan pengukuran hasil pembelajaran secara objektif serta reka bentuk kajian perbandingan yang lebih kukuh dalam bilik darjah bahasa Inggeris sebagai bahasa kedua (ESL).

items.title: Supporting Researcher Control in AI-Assisted Social Media Analysis: A Mixed-Methods Study of AI4OSN
items.abstract: High-quality annotated datasets are critical for advancing computational social science (CSS) research, yet collecting, curating, and analyzing large-scale data from dynamic sources such as online social networks (OSNs) remains a persistent bottleneck. Researchers must also translate substantive questions into queries, relevance criteria, and defensible interpretations. Large language models (LLMs) can assist, but they can also obscure the judgments, potentially reducing researcher oversight and critical evaluation. We present AI4OSN, a mixed-initiative platform that keeps researchers in control of data collection, relevance labeling, and sensemaking while making AI assistance available as an inspectable advisory resource. In a systematic user study (N=18) using X/Twitter data, participants reported above-benchmark perceived usability (mean SUS score of 79.7), increased confidence in LLM-assisted annotation and analysis tasks, and low cognitive workload during AI-supported sensemaking. Notably, novice participants showed descriptively greater alignment and higher reported agreement with AI output than experienced participants, underscoring the need to support differentiated verification practices across expertise levels. Overall, this work contributes both a human-centered system for social data analysis and empirical insights into how AI-assisted interfaces shape researcher behavior, trust, and decision-making. Our findings highlight design opportunities and tensions in building accessible, transparent, and agentic AI systems for social media and web research.

items.title: Tabular Foundation Models as Emulators for Forecasting Terrestrial Ecosystem Dynamics
items.abstract: Process-based terrestrial biosphere models such as the Ecosystem Demography (ED) model underpin global carbon budgets, but their cost limits global, high-resolution and scenario-rich simulation. Deep emulators such as DeepED reduce that cost but require task-specific architectures and training. Tabular foundation models offer a different route: TabPFN predicts new rows by in-context learning, without being trained on the task. We compare TabPFN-3.5 with two DeepED baselines, $DeepED_{LSTM}$ and $DeepED_{Transformer}$, on CarbonGlobe's overall evaluation, which trains on a uniform 1/16 sample of sites and tests on the other 50,779, predicting the 40-year state of all seven ED outputs. We then test every model, trained on present-day data only, on ED runs forced by SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 for 2021--2060 in six continental forest regions. With no training, TabPFN-3.5 has the lowest present-day height error of the three models and is within 4% of $DeepED_{LSTM}$ for soil carbon, but is less accurate for AGB, LAI and the carbon fluxes. In 2060, errors are several times larger than at the same sites under present-day forcing, and every model underestimates the biomass that ED gains. Under SSP5-8.5, TabPFN-3.5 is the most accurate model for height, AGB, soil carbon and LAI, with the lowest AGB error in all six regions, although, unlike ED, it predicts no larger biomass gain than under SSP1-2.6. Under SSP1-2.6, no model is best overall.

items.title: TAMA: A Human–AI Collaborative Thematic Analysis Framework Using Multi-Agent LLMs for Clinical Interviews
items.abstract: Thematic analysis (TA) is a widely used qualitative approach for uncovering latent meanings in unstructured text data. TA provides valuable insights in healthcare but is resource-intensive. Large Language Models (LLMs) have been introduced to perform TA, yet their applications in high-stakes healthcare settings, particularly for qualitative clinical interview analysis, remain limited. Here, we propose TAMA : A Human–AI Collaborative TA framework using M ulti- A gent LLMs for clinical interviews. We leverage the scalability and coherence of multi-agent systems through structured conversations between agents and coordinate the expertise of cardiac experts in TA. Using interview transcripts from parents of children with Anomalous Aortic Origin of a Coronary Artery (AAOCA), a rare congenital heart disease, we demonstrate that TAMA outperforms single-agent LLM TA approaches, achieving higher thematic hit rate, coverage, and distinctiveness. TAMA demonstrates strong potential for automated TA in clinical settings by leveraging multi-agent LLM systems with human-in-the-loop integration by enhancing quality while significantly reducing manual workload. The full implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Charlie-Yi-SJ/TAMA .

items.title: Task-level assessment of robotic solutions in warehouses: a human-centric framework
items.abstract: Technological advancements are transforming warehouse operations, as robotic solutions are increasingly deployed to enhance efficiency and productivity. Although these technologies reduce physical strain and automate repetitive tasks, their broader effects on human factors (HFs), including perceptual, mental, physical, and psychosocial dimensions, remain insufficiently understood. Moreover, explicit links between specific robotic capabilities and task-level effects on workers remain limited. To address this gap, this study develops a human-centric, task-level framework for evaluating how different robotic solutions influence HFs in warehouse operations. Using an exploratory, qualitative, multi-method approach, the study triangulates insights from literature, practitioner discussions, robotics solution providers, and end users to classify robotic solutions according to interaction level, task-execution roles, and adaptability. Application of the framework to the key warehouse task of order picking shows that robotic solutions reduce physical workload while introducing mixed mental and perceptual demands related to supervision and monitoring, and psychosocial challenges associated with shared-space interaction and job engagement. These findings highlight the importance of early human-centric evaluation during technology selection and implementation, enabling organisations to anticipate potential benefits and challenges prior to deployment. The framework supports human-centric decision-making in warehouse robotics and provides a basis for future empirical research on task-level human–robot interaction (HRI).

items.title: Teachers’ Perceptions about Digitalization of Teaching and its Influence on Students’ Engagement at GS Kagugu, Rwanda
items.abstract: The digitalization of teaching has become a global educational priority aimed at enhancing student engagement and promoting learner-centered instruction.In Rwanda, national initiatives such as the ICT in Education Policy and Smart Classroom Project seek to integrate digital technologies into classroom practices.However, limited evidence exists regarding teachers' perceptions of digitalization and its influence on student engagement at the school level.This qualitative case study explored secondary school teachers' perceptions of the digitalization of teaching and its influence on students' behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement at GS Kagugu in Gasabo District, Rwanda.Guided by Constructivist Learning Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the study employed an interpretivist paradigm using semi-structured interviews and document analysis.Five purposively selected teachers from different subject areas participated in the study.Thematic analysis revealed that teachers conceptualize digitalization either as the substitution of traditional instructional tools or as a pedagogical transformation that promotes learner-centered and interactive learning.The findings indicated that digital teaching practices positively influence student motivation, participation, attention, and conceptual understanding when effectively integrated.However, challenges including unstable internet connectivity, power interruptions, limited digital competencies, and inadequate professional development constrain meaningful technology integration.The study recommends continuous school-based professional development, peer-led mentoring initiatives, equitable access to digital resources, and the provision of localized offline-capable digital learning materials.Educational digitalization should therefore prioritize teacher capacity building alongside technological investments to maximize student engagement and learning outcomes.

items.title: Teaching Fast, High-Precision Skills in Mixed Reality: A Terminal Feedback System for Iaido
items.abstract: Mixed Reality (MR) movement applications for consumers are mostly games and exergames, while research systems that target skill acquisition typically rely on external motion capture or enterprise headsets. Fast, ballistic motions such as a sword strike are completed too quickly to correct mid-movement, so motor-learning theory favors terminal over concurrent feedback. We present a first-person MR system for the unmodified Meta Quest 3 that captures a full strike, compares it against a demonstrator’s reference, and delivers terminal feedback: Knowledge of Performance (KP), a line-based visualization of path and blade-orientation error, and Knowledge of Result (KR), a summary verdict. Iaido, a Japanese sword-drawing art whose strikes demand both a correct path and an aligned cutting edge, serves as the precision testbed. In a within-subjects crossover study (n = 16), novices practiced with and without this feedback, each block followed by an immediate feedback-free post-test, and reported workload (NASA-TLX) and intrinsic motivation (IMI). During guided practice, blade-angle error was lower than during unguided practice (Δ = −6.7°, p = 0.010, dz = −0.74). At the post-test it was lower but not significant (dz = −0.56); delayed retention was not tested. Path deviation was lower but not significant, with the residual error mainly in depth along the line of sight. Workload was higher but not significantly so, and intrinsic motivation stayed high. These results point to an accuracy–workload trade-off for reference-based terminal feedback in fast-motion MR training, established against unassisted practice, which simulates self-training.

items.title: The (Im)Proficiency of Firearms Examiners
items.abstract: For decades, the nation’s largest provider of forensic proficiency tests, Collaborative Testing Services, structured its firearms examination exercises around bullet and cartridge case comparisons so simplistic as to nearly guarantee vanishingly low misidentification rates. Practitioners, in turn, enthusiastically relied on these results during increasingly vigorous admissibility challenges to defend their alleged ability—using little more than their training, experience, and subjective judgment—to divine the precise gun used in a crime. By and large, they succeeded. Although outside scholars (lawyers, statisticians, human factors experts, and more) have remained constant in their criticisms of the field’s methods and the design of its efforts to measure accuracy (in the form of proficiency testing and beyond), untroubled admissibility and untroubled qualification of firearms examiners as “experts” have remained the norm. In 2023, however, CTS (albeit unintentionally) bucked the trend of simplistic testing, releasing an exercise, CTS 23–5262, that forced participants to confront damaged and poorly marked bullets. The results should trouble even those unfamiliar with firearms examination and the debates about its validity. Although the questioned bullets provided to participants were not fired by the same gun as the exemplar bullets in their packets, 22% of test takers failed by “matching” at least one questioned item to the exemplars, and participants on the whole committed misidentifications 37.4% of the time they offered definitive conclusions about the source of the “challenging” bullets in the proficiency test. To highlight the importance of these results, and to emphasize the extent they depart from past proficiency tests, this Article both analyzes CTS bullet exercises dating back to 2006 and dives deeply into CTS 23–5262 itself. Examiners’ performance failures on the latter, this Article ultimately argues, (1) contradict claims that analysts will rarely err when assessing the source of fired ammunition; (2) raise questions about the validity of comparisons performed on damaged bullets; and (3) force litigants and the courts to grapple with the significance of test error when qualifying individual examiners as experts. Indeed, given how grossly CTS 23–5262 runs counter to the claims made by defenders of firearms examination (and the judges who have parroted them), it may be that the test can (or at least should) finally push the field over the edge and out of criminal courts.

items.title: The Conservator as Digital Content Creator: A Human-in-the-Loop Gamification Framework for Child-Centered Museum Communication
items.abstract: Communicating conservation science to children requires transforming highly technical documentation into accessible, engaging, and scientifically reliable narratives. This paper presents a human in the loop framework that formalizes conservation documentation as epistemic ground truth and employs Generative AI exclusively for controlled narrative adaptation. The conservator retains full editorial authority, ensuring epistemic reliability and ethical compliance. The methodology is demonstrated through three comparative case studies implemented on freely-accessible/no-code platforms, Animaker, Genially, and Lumi Education/H5P, representing animated storytelling with puzzles, interactive flip card discovery, and quiz based reinforcement. The paper outlines future directions for evaluating the clarity and accessibility of the digital narratives within museum contexts. As part of an ongoing doctoral dissertation, the work outlines core research questions, methodological milestones, and future directions, including the release of an open repository to support reproducibility. The framework contributes a scalable, low-barrier model for responsible AI-assisted communication of conservation knowledge in museum contexts.
